Partie 2 Titre: The amphiphilic molecule: a molecular gripper
Partie 2 Contenu:
The secret of soap lies in the chemical structure of its components: the <surfactants>. Each soap molecule is described as **amphiphilic**, which means it has two ends with opposite properties. On one side, a **hydrophilic head** ("water-loving") and on the other, a long **hydrophobic tail** ("water-fearing") but lipophilic ("fat-loving").

During washing, a molecular battle begins. The hydrophobic tails of the soap molecules desperately seek to flee the water flowing from the tap. Upon encountering a virus, they brutally insert themselves into its lipid membrane, like crowbars driving into a wooden partition. 

The accumulation of these molecules within the viral envelope creates such pressure that it eventually **disintegrates** the virus's structure. Viral fats are then captured in the center of small soap spheres called **micelles**. Once the virus is thus dismantled, its components are nothing more than harmless debris that the rinsing water easily carries away. This process is a pure physical destruction, leaving no chance for mutation or resistance for the virus.
Partie 3 Titre: Mechanical action and contact time
Partie 3 Contenu:
The effectiveness of washing does not rely solely on chemistry, but also on the mechanical action of rubbing. It takes about **20 seconds** for soap molecules to effectively penetrate all skin folds and saturate the membranes of every viral particle present on the skin.

Rubbing helps dislodge viruses that adhere to the skin thanks to electrochemical forces. Soap acts here as a lubricant that lowers the surface tension of water, allowing it to wet more surfaces, including under the fingernails and in the finger joints. 

This is the major difference with **hydroalcoholic gel**. While alcohol denatures proteins and also dissolves lipids, it does not physically remove debris. Against naked viruses, which have no lipid envelope to dissolve, the gel is often less effective than soap. Washing with soap indeed combines two actions: chemical destruction for enveloped viruses and mechanical expulsion for all types of micro-organisms.
Partie 4 Titre: {Soap has existed since at least 2800 B.C. The Babylonians mixed water, alkali, and cassia oil to create a cleansing paste, long before understanding the very notion of microbes.}
Partie 4 Contenu: Soap vs Gel: choosing the right weapon

Intro:
In September 1928, the Scottish physician **Alexander Fleming** returned from vacation and prepared to clean his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital in London. He discovered that one of his bacterial cultures had been invaded by a microscopic fungus. Rather than throwing away the infected dish, he observed a phenomenon that would revolutionize modern medicine and double human life expectancy.

[Alexander Fleming penicillin Petri dish]

This discovery, the result of chance and an observant mind, marks the birth of the era of antibiotics.
Partie 1 Titre: The serendipity of a bacteriologist
Partie 1 Contenu:
**Alexander Fleming** (1881-1955) was not a researcher with rigid methods; legend has it that his laboratory was in a state of permanent mess. In **September 1928**, he was studying **Staphylococcus**, formidable bacteria causing abscesses, septicemia, and often fatal pneumonia.

One of his Petri dishes was contaminated by a greenish mold: **Penicillium notatum**. Fleming noticed a **zone of inhibition** (a clear zone) around the fungus: the bacteria did not survive in contact with it. He deduced that the mold secreted a substance capable of inhibiting bacterial growth. He named this culture broth **penicillin**.

Despite his initial enthusiasm, Fleming encountered a major obstacle: the instability of the molecule. Penicillin was extremely difficult to isolate in a pure and concentrated form. For nearly ten years, it remained a simple scientific curiosity that Fleming used only to facilitate the culture of certain resistant bacteria in the laboratory.

{The Penicillium notatum that contaminated Fleming's dish probably came from a mycology laboratory located on the floor below the same building, traveling through the stairs or air ducts.}
Partie 2 Titre: The Oxford turning point and the urgency of war
Partie 2 Contenu:
The transition from the experimental stage to a usable drug did only begin from **1938**. Two researchers from the University of Oxford, **<Howard Florey>** and **Ernst Boris Chain**, rediscovered Fleming's work. They understood that the potential of this substance was immense, but that it required expertise in biochemistry that Fleming did not have.

In **1940**, the Oxford team achieved the impossible: purifying penicillin and testing its effectiveness on mice infected with streptococci. The results were definitive: penicillin cured where all other treatments failed. The first human test in **1941** on an English policeman, though tragic (the patient died because the stocks of penicillin ran out before full recovery), proved the non-toxicity and effectiveness of the product.

The **Second World War** acted as a powerful catalyst. Faced with the slaughter of war infections (**gangrene**, infected wounds), the Allies made penicillin production a national priority, almost equal to the atomic project. Unable to produce massively under German bombs, Florey's team went to the United States to seek help from the chemical **Giants**.

[penicillin antibiotic production laboratory]
Partie 3 Titre: Toward industrial mass production
Partie 3 Contenu:
The industrialization of penicillin was an unprecedented technological feat. Between **1943** and **1945**, production rose from a few milligrams to hundreds of billions of units per month. American engineers developed deep fermentation in 30,000-liter columns, replacing the thousands of milk bottles initially used at Oxford.

At the time of the **Normandy Landings** in June 1944, stocks were sufficient to treat every wounded soldier. This medical advance gave a heroic tactical and moral advantage to the Allies. For the first time in the history of conflicts, fewer soldiers died from their infections than from the direct impact of their wounds.

After the war, access to penicillin became democratized, radically transforming the global pathological landscape. Once-deadly diseases such as **Syphilis** or **scarlet fever** became curable in a few days, bringing humanity into an era of unprecedented health optimism.

{In the early days of production, penicillin was so rare that the urine of treated patients was collected to filter it and reuse the drug, as 80% of the dose is excreted by the body within a few hours.}
Partie 4 Titre: Fleming's legacy and the challenge of resistance
Partie 4 Contenu:
In **1945**, the Nobel Prize in Medicine crowned the trio of Fleming, Florey, and Chain. However, during his acceptance speech, Fleming chose to warn humanity rather than simply celebrate his victory. He prophesied that if antibiotics were poorly dosed or used abusively, microbes would eventually learn to resist them.

This premonitory analysis defines the **Concept** of **<antibiotic resistance>**. Naturally, through Darwinian selection, bacteria mutate to survive treatments. Today, the intensive use of antibiotics in human medicine and livestock farming has accelerated this process. **Multidrug-resistant bacteria** now complicate even the most routine hospital care.

Despite this contemporary challenge, the global impact is dizzying: it is estimated that penicillin has saved more than **200 million lives** since its discovery. It opened the way to a whole family of antibiotics (cephalosporins, macrolides) which today constitute the backbone of modern medicine.

|| In 1928, a Petri dish forgotten by Fleming became, thanks to the industrialization driven by the Second World War, the first miracle cure in history, spectacularly increasing world life expectancy. ||

Titre: The discovery of electricity and its applications
Intro: Electricity was not «invented» by man: it is a fundamental force of the universe that we spent millennia identifying, then centuries taming. From the observation of static phenomena by Greek scholars to the implementation of global high-voltage networks, this History is one of a conquest of the invisible. It rests on the genius of pioneers like **Franklin**, **Faraday**, **Maxwell** or **Tesla**, whose Work allowed for the transformation of a simple laboratory curiosity into an engine of modern industrial civilization. This narrative explores the trajectory of this energy, from the sky to our power outlets.
Partie 1 Titre: From Greek origins to Franklin: capturing lightning
Partie 1 Contenu:
The history of electricity begins with a simple tactile observation. Since Antiquity, the Greeks noticed that **yellow amber**, a fossilized resin, attracts light objects like feathers when rubbed with animal skin. This phenomenon, which we call static electricity today, takes its name from the Greek word for amber: <elektron>.

Yet, it wasn't until the 18th century that the deep nature of this phenomenon was understood. In **1752**, the American **Benjamin Franklin** postulated that the lightning observed during storms was not divine anger, but a massive transfer of electrical charges. To prove it, he performed his iconic experiment: he flew a **kite with a metal key** attached to the string during a storm.

[Benjamin Franklin kite lightning experiment]

{Benjamin Franklin conducted his kite experiment in 1752 - but it was extremely dangerous. A Russian professor tried to reproduce it the same year and was killed by lightning.}

Franklin thus proved that lightning is static electricity on an atmospheric scale. This major advance led immediately to the invention of the **lightning rod**, intended to channel these flows toward the ground. A few decades later, in **1800**, the Italian physicist **Alessandro Volta** took a crucial step by inventing the first **electric battery** (the **voltaic pile**). By stacking zinc and copper discs separated by cardboard soaked in <brine>, he managed to create a continuous electrical current, opening the era of electrochemistry.
Partie 2 Titre: Faraday and the equations of the invisible
Partie 2 Contenu:
While Volta's battery allowed for the production of current, it remained limited to low chemical powers. The real revolution occurred in the 1830s thanks to the intuitive genius of **<Michael Faraday>**. Coming from a modest and self-taught background, Faraday understood that electricity and magnetism are two facets of the same physical reality.

In **1831**, he highlighted the Principle of **electromagnetic induction**: by moving a magnet near a conductive wire, he noticed that an electric current was generated in the wire. This discovery is the foundation of all our current technology because it allows the transformation of mechanical Movement into electricity.

[Faraday electromagnetic induction experiment]

The consequences were immediate: if one can produce electricity through Movement, one can build **generators** (transforming the Movement of water or steam into current) and **motors** (using current to create Movement). This symmetry is the basis of heavy industry.

Faraday's conceptual rigor was completed in **1865** by the Scotsman **James Clerk Maxwell**. The latter formulated a set of mathematical equations, **Maxwell's equations**, which unify the Laws of electricity and magnetism into a single force: **electromagnetism**. Maxwell also predicted the existence of radio waves, proving that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.
Partie 3 Titre: The confrontation: Edison vs Tesla
Partie 3 Contenu:
At the end of the 19th century, electricity left the laboratories to take to the streets. It was the beginning of the **« <War of the currents (Edison vs Tesla)> »**, an unprecedented industrial and technical conflict pitting two visions of the World against each other. On one side, **Thomas Edison**, a prolific inventor and formidable businessman, advocated for **direct current** (DC). On the Other, **Nikola Tesla**, a visionary Serbian genius supported by **George Westinghouse**, defended **alternating current** (AC).

[Tesla Edison electric power station]

Edison had the first network installed in New York. However, direct current had a major physical limit: it could not be transported more than a few kilometers without a massive loss of energy in the form of heat. Conversely, Tesla's alternating current could be raised to very high voltages thanks to transformers, allowing it to be transported over hundreds of kilometers with exceptional efficiency.

Seeing himself losing the market, Edison launched an aggressive press campaign to discredit alternating current, presenting it as deadly. He went as far as organizing public electrocutions of animals. But the technical superiority of Tesla's system was undeniable. In **1893**, at the Chicago World's Fair, and later with the equipment of Niagara Falls with AC generators, alternating current definitively established itself as the global standard.
Partie 4 Titre: The electrification of the World and new challenges
Partie 4 Contenu:
The 20th century saw electricity become the backbone of Modernity. It no longer served only for public lighting, but now powered homes, means of transport and, later, computing electronics. This universal accessibility was made possible by the standardization of national networks based on alternating current, but it also created a total energy dependence.

Technological evolution accelerated with the invention of the **transistor** in **1947**, which uses the electrical properties of certain materials to process information. This was the shift from power electricity (heating, moving) to information electricity (digital). Today, the stakes have shifted toward carbon-free production and storage.

{The Serbian engineer Nikola Tesla, despite his 300 patents, died poor and alone in a hotel room in New York, preferring scientific research to commercial profit.}

Storing electricity remains one of the most complex technological frontiers. Unlike coal or oil, electricity is difficult to store on a large scale, forcing network managers to balance production and consumption in real time. The transition to renewable energies and the electric vehicle gives all its relevance today to Volta's research on batteries.

|| B to remember: Electricity was tamed over two centuries: Franklin revealed its nature in 1752, Faraday invented the electric machine in 1831, before Tesla won the war of the currents against Edison, imposing the alternating standard that still powers our world. ||

Intro: On **November 8, 1895**, in the darkness of a laboratory at the University of Würzburg, the German physicist **Wilhelm Röntgen** observed a phenomenon that would revolutionize the understanding of matter and medical diagnosis. By discovering an invisible radiation capable of passing through opaque bodies, he broke the limits of human vision and opened the era of internal imaging without surgery. This advance, rewarded with the first Nobel Prize in History, marks the starting point of a radical transformation in clinical practice and the sciences of matter.
Partie 1 Titre: The Würzburg accident: invisible light
Partie 1 Contenu:
The physicist **Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen** was conducting research on high-voltage electrical currents using a **Crookes tube**. This device is a vacuum glass bulb in which electrons are projected from a <cathode> toward an <anode>. In order to study luminescence without being disturbed by stray light, Röntgen wrapped his tube in thick black cardboard.

As he activated the device, he noticed that a screen covered with **barium platinocyanide**, located more than two meters away, emitted a fluorescent glow. Intrigued by this radiation that seemed to pass through the black cardboard, he placed various objects between the tube and the screen: a book, a deck of cards, then a wooden box. Each time, the shadow cast on the screen revealed the internal structure of the objects.

Naming this unknown energy **«X-rays»**, he decided to test the effect on human tissue. On December 22, 1895, he performed the first **X-ray** in History by exposing the hand of his wife, Bertha, to a photographic plate for fifteen minutes. The image distinctly showed the phalanges and a wedding ring floating around the metacarpus.

[Wilhelm Röntgen X-ray hand 1895]

{Upon seeing the image of her own bones, Bertha Röntgen reportedly exclaimed: «I have seen my own death!», because at that time, seeing a human skeleton was inseparable from the image of passing away.}

The image stunned the scientific community because it proved that the human body can become transparent under the effect of these high-energy electromagnetic waves.
Partie 2 Titre: The diagnostic revolution and military use
Partie 2 Contenu:
As soon as his work was published on **December 28, 1895**, the news spread with lightning speed. Unlike many inventors, Röntgen refused to patent his discovery, believing it belonged to humanity. This generosity allowed for the immediate adoption of the technology in hospitals around the World, where surgery—hitherto "blind"—suddenly became image-guided.

Doctors used X-rays to diagnose complex fractures or identify lung abnormalities linked to tuberculosis. Before this invention, locating a foreign body in the organism required exploratory incisions that were often fatal due to infections. With radiography, the surgical act became precise and targeted.

[early X-ray medical radiograph]

The real mass test occurred during the **First World War**. Faced with the massive influx of wounded, the need for rapid imaging became vital. This is where **Marie Curie** stepped in, understanding that transporting the wounded to fixed radiology centers was too risky. She then designed mobile units, the <"Petites Curies" during World War I>, equipped with dynamos and radiology equipment. These trucks allowed for the extraction of shrapnel and bullets on the battlefield, saving tens of thousands of soldiers from amputation or death by <gangrene>.
Partie 3 Titre: Fatal invisibility: the price of radiation
Partie 3 Contenu:
Despite the enthusiasm, the end of the 19th century ignored the **dangers of ionizing radiation**. Physicists and doctors handled X-rays without any protection, often placing their own hands under the beam to calibrate the devices. This prolonged exposure caused <radiodermitis>, severe skin burns that frequently degenerated into skin cancers or <leukemias>.

Pioneers like **Clarence Dally**, Thomas Edison's assistant, died in excruciating pain after multiple amputations, victims of their scientific curiosity. Edison himself, traumatized by the death of his friend and his own visual troubles, abandoned his research on X-rays, stating they were too dangerous to be handled without fear.

At the same time, Röntgen's discovery acted as a catalyst for other breakthroughs. In 1896, seeking a relationship between fluorescence and X-rays, **Henri Becquerel** observed that uranium salts spontaneously emitted similar rays without an external energy source. He had just discovered natural <Radioactivity and early risks>. This discovery would be the foundation of the work of **Pierre and Marie Curie**, who would isolate polonium and radium, also paying a heavy health price for their research.

{In the 1930s-1950s, some shoe stores offered X-ray fluoroscopes to see one's feet inside shoes - without any protection. These machines were not banned until the late 1960s.}
Partie 4 Titre: Modern legacy and the structuring of the invisible
Partie 4 Contenu:
Today, X-rays are no longer limited to the simple detection of fractures. They are at the heart of **computed tomography** (CT scan), which allows for the reconstruction of three-dimensional images of the human body in successive slices. This technology, coupled with computing, offers millimeter precision for detecting tumors or strokes at their first signs.

Beyond medicine, X-ray radiation has become an indispensable tool for astronomy and security. Space telescopes track X-ray sources in space to identify <black holes> or <supernovae> explosions, while airports use these waves to inspect luggage. In the field of Art, experts use radiography to discover hidden sketches under the layers of paint of the great masters.

Röntgen's discovery thus transformed the opacity of the world into an exploitable transparency. It allowed for the understanding that the human eye is only capable of perceiving a tiny fraction of the electromagnetic spectrum. By breaking free from this biological limit, humanity acquired an investigative power that extends from the heart of the atom to the edges of the universe.

|| Röntgen discovered X-rays on November 8, 1895, by accident; in less than a decade, they became the most powerful diagnostic tool in History, laying the foundations for modern nuclear physics. ||

Titre: The discovery of the microwave (by accident)
Intro: In 1945, at the end of the Second World War, technological innovation was at its peak, driven by the war effort. It is in this context of military research that a banal observation - the melting of a candy - would revolutionize kitchens throughout the World. This discovery, purely by chance, transformed a precision detection instrument, the radar, into a now-indispensable household appliance. This course explores how the ingenuity of an American engineer allowed for the taming of electromagnetic waves to heat our food, moving from a 340 kg prototype to the small box present on our countertops.
Partie 1 Titre: Percy Spencer and the spark of chance
Partie 1 Contenu:
The history of wave cooking begins with <Percy Spencer>, an engineer recognized for his practical genius. In **1945**, he worked for the **Raytheon** company, a pillar of the arms industry. His mission consisted of improving **magnetrons**, electronic components capable of producing short-length radio waves, essential for the operation of air defense radars.

While performing tests near an active magnetron, Spencer felt an unusual sensation of heat in his pocket. To his great surprise, he found that his **chocolate bar** had completely melted, while the surrounding room remained cool. Unlike others who would have ignored the incident, his scientific curiosity pushed him to conduct immediate experiments.

[Percy Spencer microwave discovery radar]

The next day, he placed **popcorn** in front of the device and watched the kernels pop in seconds. He then tried the experiment with a fresh egg which, under the pressure of internal steam generated by the waves, ended up exploding. Spencer instantly understood that he had just discovered a new way to transfer thermal energy, not by external conduction like a fire, but by an internal excitation of matter.
Partie 2 Titre: The challenge of miniaturization and cost
Partie 2 Contenu:
Transforming a laboratory discovery into a mass consumption product was a long and costly process. In **1947**, Raytheon marketed the first model, named the **Radarange**. For the time, it was a technological colossus: it stood **1.8 meters high** and weighed nearly **340 kg**. 

[first microwave oven Radarange 1947]

Its price was just as colossal, amounting at the time to about $5,000, or the equivalent of **$56,000 today**. Due to its size, price, and the need for a complex water-cooling system, the device was initially reserved for industrial kitchens, luxury restaurants, and large ocean liners like the SS United States.

The breakthrough for the general public did not occur until the late 1960s. In **1967**, Raytheon's subsidiary Amana launched the first countertop model, the **Radarange RR-1**, sold for $495. This drastic reduction in size and cost was made possible by the improvement of electronic circuits and the replacement of liquid cooling with an air ventilation system.

{The first customer of the Radarange was a Boston restaurant that wanted to test the fast cooking of hot dogs to reduce customer wait times during lunch service.}

Mass democratization took place in the 1970s thanks to the arrival of Japanese manufacturers who standardized production, bringing the microwave below the symbolic entry-level price threshold.
Partie 3 Titre: The physical mechanism of molecular agitation
Partie 3 Contenu:
The operation of the oven is based on the emission of <microwaves>, low-energy waves that sit between infrared and radio waves. The <standard frequency> of 2.45 GHz was chosen because it offers an ideal compromise: it is low enough to penetrate to the heart of food, but high enough to be absorbed efficiently by <water molecules>.

These molecules are called polar, meaning they possess a positive charge at one end and a negative charge at the other, like tiny magnets. Under the effect of the electromagnetic field that changes direction billions of times per second, the <water molecules> attempt to align with the field. This ultra-fast rotation creates intense molecular friction.

{They are called "microwaves" not because they are tiny in absolute terms, but because they are much shorter than the classic radio waves used at the time of their discovery, which could measure several kilometers.}

It is this friction that produces heat. Contrary to a popular misconception, the microwave does not heat from the inside out in the strict sense, but it simultaneously heats all areas containing water. Materials like glass or ceramic, devoid of free <water molecules>, allow the waves to pass through without heating up themselves.

Metal, on the other hand, is an electrical conductor. The waves induce massive surface currents in it. If the metal has points or thin edges (like the tines of a fork), charges accumulate there until they ionize the air, creating spectacular and dangerous electrical arcs for the device.
Partie 4 Titre: A major societal impact
Partie 4 Contenu:
Beyond the technical feat, the microwave has profoundly changed eating habits and social organization. It favored the rise of ready-made meals and allowed for greater individual flexibility within the home, allowing each family member to eat at different times.

The food industry adapted by creating specific packaging and optimized recipes for this cooking method. While some nutritionists initially feared a loss of vitamins, studies show that the speed of cooking and the small amount of water used often better preserve nutrients than traditional boiling.

Today, the device is present in more than **90%** of households in developed countries. It remains the symbol of an era where speed and convenience have become domestic priorities, transforming a radar surveillance tool into an ally of daily life.

|| The microwave oven was born in 1945 from a chance observation by Percy Spencer, whose chocolate bar had melted near a military radar, leading to the invention of cooking by molecular agitation. ||

Intro: In 1687, the English physicist **Isaac Newton** published the <Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica>, a work that would radically transform our understanding of the cosmos. In a few hundred pages, he managed to unify two worlds previously considered distinct: terrestrial physics, governed by change and falling, and celestial physics, perceived as perfect and eternal. By proposing a mathematical model capable of explaining both the fall of an apple and the ballet of the planets, Newton founded **classical mechanics** and laid the foundations of modern science.
Partie 1 Titre: The context: astronomy before the synthesis
Partie 1 Contenu:
Before the 17th century, astronomy was essentially descriptive. While we knew how to predict eclipses and the Movement of luminous points in the sky, we were ignorant of the dynamic cause. The revolution began with **Copernicus** who, in 1543, dared to place the Sun at the center of the system, breaking the dogma of <geocentrism>.

A few decades later, <Johannes Kepler> passed a crucial milestone. By analyzing the observational data of his predecessor <Tycho Brahe>, he formulated his three laws of planetary Movement between 1609 and 1619. He demonstrated in particular that planets do not rotate in perfect circles, but along **elliptical orbits**. However, Kepler himself did not understand what physical engine forced the planets to follow these precise trajectories.

Simultaneously, in Italy, **Galileo** studied the Movement of objects on Earth. He was the first to theorize the **isochronism** of falling bodies: in a vacuum, a feather and a lead ball hit the ground simultaneously. He thus laid the foundations of modern dynamics, but he lacked the link to escape the Earth's atmosphere. The fundamental question remained: is there an invisible force connecting all objects in the universe?

{Newton wrote more texts on alchemy and biblical interpretation of the Temple of Solomon than on physics or mathematics, disciplines for which he is nonetheless world-famous.}
Partie 2 Titre: The law of universal gravitation
Partie 2 Contenu:
The anecdote of the apple, though often simplified, possesses a kernel of historical truth. It was during a forced stay at his family home because of the plague (1665-1666) that Newton observed a fruit fall in his garden at Woolsthorpe. His genius was not discovering that objects fall, but wondering if the force that attracts the apple could not extend all the way to the Moon.

[Isaac Newton apple tree Woolsthorpe]

His **Law of universal gravitation** stipulates that every body possessing a mass exerts an attractive force on every other body. This force is proportional to the **product of their masses** and inversely proportional to the **Square of the distance** separating them. Mathematically, this means that if two objects move twice their initial distance apart, the attraction between them is divided by four.

This Law is an unprecedented unification. Newton demonstrated that the Moon is actually in 'permanent fall' around the Earth: its lateral speed prevents it from crashing, but gravity keeps it in its orbit. He proved mathematically that this mutual attraction imposes on the planets the elliptical shapes that Kepler had observed empirically.

[planets orbit solar system gravity]

By reconciling heaven and earth under a single equation, Newton gave birth to the idea of a **mechanical universe**, predictable and ordered like a giant clock of which God would be the great architect.

{Outside of his research, Newton was Master of the Royal Mint and pursued counterfeiters with such rigor that he had several of them hanged.}
Partie 3 Titre: The three laws of movement and classical mechanics
Partie 3 Contenu:
To structure his theory of gravitation, Newton had to define the fundamental rules of Movement, known today as **Newton's laws**. The first is the principle of **Inertia**: a body only changes its state of Movement if an external force is exerted upon it. The second establishes the fundamental relationship of dynamics: force is equal to the product of mass times acceleration (**F=ma**). Finally, the third Law poses the principle of **action and reaction**: every force exerted by a body A on a body B generates an equal and opposite force from body B on body A.

These principles founded **classical mechanics**, which reigned supreme over the sciences for more than two centuries. Thanks to them, humanity was able not only to understand the cosmos but also to transform the Earth. All structural calculations for bridges, the design of engines during the industrial revolution, and even the trajectory calculations for military ballistics rely on these Newtonian foundations.

The effectiveness of Newton's model was such that in the 19th century, the astronomer Urbain Le Verrier was able to predict the existence of an unknown planet, **Neptune**, simply by observing the gravitational perturbations experienced by Uranus. This discovery was the ultimate triumph of Newtonian physics.

{In 1816, one of Newton's teeth was sold at auction for the modern equivalent of $35,000; the buyer had it mounted on a ring.}
Partie 4 Titre: Legacy and limits of the Newtonian vision
Partie 4 Contenu:
Despite its extraordinary precision at the human and planetary scale, Newton's Theory presented a major conceptual flaw: it did not explain the *mechanism* of gravity. Newton himself said: 'I frame no hypotheses' (<Hypotheses non fingo>). He noted the force but could not explain how such an attraction could act instantaneously across the vacuum of space.

It was the revolution of **relativistic gravitation (Einstein)** at the beginning of the 20th century that brought the answer. <Albert Einstein> understood that gravity is not an 'invisible force' acting at a distance, but a modification of the geometry of space itself. The mass of a celestial body curves the fabric of space-time, like a bowling ball would deform a stretched tablecloth, forcing Other objects to follow these curves.

Today, while we use Newtonian mechanics to send probes to explore the solar system, we must use Einstein's corrections for the daily operation of our **GPS**. Newton's Theory has therefore not become 'false'; it has simply become a special case of a broader physical reality, valid as long as masses are not too massive and speeds are well below that of light.

{Although Einstein modernized gravity, NASA engineers used only Newton's equations to calculate Apollo 11's trajectory to the Moon.}

|| Newton published in 1687 a single Law that explains both the fall of an apple and the Movement of planets thanks to the laws of classical mechanics. ||

Intro: **Marie Curie** is a monumental figure in the history of sciences, whose exceptional destiny shattered the glass ceilings of her time. She remains the first woman to have received a Nobel Prize, and the only person in the World to have been honored in two distinct scientific disciplines: physics and chemistry. Her hard work, conducted under precarious conditions, not only led to the discovery of new chemical elements but, above all, brought about a total paradigm shift: the understanding that the atom, far from being an inert ball of matter, is a reservoir of energy capable of transforming spontaneously. This transition from classical chemistry to nuclear physics paved the way for modern medicine and atomic energy.
Partie 1 Titre: A vocation in the face of prohibitions
Partie 1 Contenu:
**Maria Sklodowska** was born in **1867** in Warsaw, in a Poland then wiped off the map and placed under Russian domination. Despite an intellectually rich family environment - her father was a professor of sciences - Maria quickly collided with the political and sexist barriers of her time. Since access to higher education was forbidden to women in Poland, she joined the **Flying University**, a clandestine and itinerant Institution that provided courses out of reach of Russian Censorship.

In **1891**, after years of savings earned as a governess, she joined her sister in Paris to enroll at the **Sorbonne**. She lived in extreme destitution, staying in a maid's room without heating, barely eating, but she managed to obtain her degrees in physics and mathematics with brilliance. It was in this research context that she met **Pierre Curie** in 1894. A brilliant physicist and expert in piezoelectricity, he saw Maria as an intellectual equal. 

Their marriage in 1895 marked the beginning of a fusion-like scientific collaboration. Pierre was not just her husband; he became her laboratory companion, sacrificing his own research to support Marie's intuitions. Together, they decided to explore an anomaly recently discovered by a colleague, unaware that they were about to shake the foundations of modern science.

{Even today, Marie Curie's notebooks are so radioactive that they are kept in lead-lined boxes at the Bibliothèque Nationale de France and can only be consulted wearing a protective suit.}
Partie 2 Titre: The invention of radioactivity
Partie 2 Contenu:
In **1896**, <Henri Becquerel> noticed that uranium salts darkened photographic plates, even when protected from light. Marie Curie chose this phenomenon as her doctoral thesis subject. Her genius lay in her method: she used the piezoelectric quartz electrometer invented by Pierre to precisely measure the electric current produced by air made conductive by uranium radiation.

She established a revolutionary observation: the intensity of the radiation depends exclusively on the **quantity of uranium**, regardless of its temperature or molecular structure. She concluded that radioactivity is an intrinsic property of the atom itself, and not the result of an external chemical reaction. This finding marks the birth of the Concept of **radioactive decay**.

[Marie Curie pitchblende radioactivity]

By analyzing **Pitchblende**, a raw uranium ore, she found that the emitted radiation was much higher than that of pure uranium. This anomaly suggested the presence of unknown elements that were much more active. In a damp, poorly ventilated shed serving as a laboratory, the Curies manually processed tons of ore residue. This Herculean Work led to the isolation of **polonium** in July 1898, so named in tribute to Marie's homeland, then of **radium** in December of the same year. Radium proved to be a million times more radioactive than uranium.

{Radium was initially seen as a miracle product: in the 1920s, it could be found in beauty creams, energy drinks, and even toothpaste before its harmful effects were understood.}
Partie 3 Titre: World recognition and sacrifice
Partie 3 Contenu:
Consecration came in **1903** with the **Nobel Prize in Physics**, shared between Becquerel and the Curies. Initially, the Nobel committee only wanted to nominate the two men, but Pierre's insistence allowed Marie's central role to be recognized. This World recognition was overshadowed in 1906 by Pierre's accidental death. Marie, devastated, refused the state pension and chose to take over her husband's teaching post, becoming the **first woman professor** at the Sorbonne.

Her career did not stop there. In **1911**, she received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for her work on the properties of radium and polonium. She was then at the height of her fame, although she suffered xenophobic and sexist press campaigns in France. 

During World War I, Marie Curie put her science at the service of the wounded. She designed the **Little Curies**, vehicles equipped with mobile X-ray equipment that allowed surgeons on the front lines to locate shrapnel in soldiers' bodies. Her constant exposure to X-rays and radioactive substances eventually destroyed her health. She died in **1934** of **Aplastic leukemia**, a bone marrow disease caused by the accumulation of radiation.

{Marie Curie's remains, transferred to the Pantheon in 1995, are enclosed in a coffin lined with lead several millimeters thick to confine the radioactivity she absorbed throughout her life.}
Partie 4 Titre: A scientific and ethical legacy
Partie 4 Contenu:
Marie Curie's legacy is colossal. On a purely scientific level, she demonstrated that elements can transform into one another, opening the way to particle physics. Her daughter, **Irène Joliot-Curie**, would continue this lineage by discovering artificial radioactivity with her husband, which also earned them a Nobel prize in 1935.

On the medical level, the discovery of radium allowed for the development of **Curietherapy**, a cancer treatment method involving the irradiation of the tumor. However, this progress showed its downside: Marie Curie herself had foreseen the dangers of handling these substances. Today, we know that <antibiotic resistance> and genetic mutations linked to radiation are major public health issues.

Finally, Marie Curie remains a model of scientific probity. The Curies consciously refused to file a **patent** for the radium extraction process, considering that scientific discoveries belong to humanity and must not serve for personal enrichment. Her archives, notebooks, and personal effects are still kept at the Bibliothèque Nationale de France under high protection.

|| Marie Curie revolutionized science by proving that radioactivity was a property of the atom, before dying a victim of her own discovery after refusing all financial profit. ||

Intro: The Internet is not the Work of a solitary inventor, but the result of technological sedimentation spread over more than **50 years**. This project, born in American military laboratories during the **Cold War**, had the initial goal of ensuring the survival of communications in the event of a nuclear conflict. Today, this monumental infrastructure connects more than **5 billion people**, having evolved from a modest network of four terminals to a planetary web governing the economy, culture, and social relations World-wide.
Partie 1 Titre: ARPANET: the Cold War as an accelerator
Partie 1 Contenu:
The History of the Internet is rooted in the technological trauma of **1957**, when the USSR launched the first artificial satellite, <Sputnik>. This shock pushed the United States to create **ARPA** (Advanced Research Projects Agency) within the Department of Defense, with the mission of getting ahead of Soviet innovations. In the 1960s, researchers imagined a communication network that would not rely on a single command center. Strategic doctrine then imposed **decentralization**: if part of the network is destroyed by an attack, the data must be able to take alternative paths to reach its destination.

This Concept resulted in the **ARPANET** project. On **October 29, 1969**, the first computer link was established between the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and the Stanford Research Institute. The transmission attempt marks History by its pioneering, though technically laborious, nature.

[ARPANET 1969 computer UCLA]

 The first message in the History of the Internet was supposed to be "LOGIN". However, the system crashed after the first two letters. The very first message transmitted was therefore simply **"LO"**.
Partie 2 Titre: TCP/IP: the invention of a universal language
Partie 2 Contenu:
During the 1970s, the challenge was no longer just connecting computers, but making different networks that spoke incompatible computer "languages" communicate with each other. This is where **Vint Cerf** and **Bob Kahn** stepped in. In **1974**, they designed a set of revolutionary protocols, **TCP/IP** (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol).

[Vint Cerf Bob Kahn internet]

This innovation is based on **packet switching**: instead of occupying an entire line for a message (like the classic telephone), information is cut into small segments. Each packet travels independently through the network and the protocol takes care of reassembling them in order upon arrival. **TCP/IP** became the official standard for ARPANET on **January 1, 1983**, a Date considered by historians as the true birth of the Internet, because it marks the transition from an experimental network to a universal infrastructure capable of aggregating any sub-network.

 The word "Internet" is short for **internetworking**, a term used to describe the technical connection between several distinct networks.
Partie 3 Titre: The World Wide Web: the human interface
Partie 3 Contenu:
Internet and the Web should not be confused. While the Internet is the physical infrastructure (cables, servers), the **World Wide Web** is the application that allows for navigating this mass of data. Between **1989 and 1991**, British physicist **Tim Berners-Lee**, a researcher at <CERN> in Geneva, developed the three pillars of the Web to facilitate document exchange between scientists: the **HTML** language for structuring pages, the **HTTP** protocol for transferring them, and **URLs** for locating them.

Aware of the scope of his invention, **Tim Berners-Lee** made a historic choice by publishing the Web's source code in the **public domain** in **1993**. By renouncing any patent or royalty, he allowed for ultra-fast World-wide adoption. From then on, navigation software like **Mosaic** transformed this textual web into a visual interface accessible to the general public, triggering the explosion of commercial and social uses we know today.

 The very first website in the World (info.cern.ch) is still viewable today. It simply explained to people what the World Wide Web was.
Partie 4 Titre: Toward a network that has become a global nervous system
Partie 4 Contenu:
From the mid-1990s, the Internet shifted from an academic tool to domestic use. The deployment of **fiber optics** and the advent of broadband radically transformed the nature of the content exchanged, allowing the transition from text to video and streaming. This technical acceleration is accompanied by a profound societal mutation: the network becomes the support for <globalization>, abolishing geographic and temporal distances.

The emergence of smartphones at the end of the 2000s marked a new stage, that of permanent and mobile internet. Today, the network integrates billions of connected objects and poses new challenges in terms of **digital sovereignty**, personal data protection, and environmental impact. From a military survival project, the Internet has become the vital infrastructure, the true nervous system of contemporary civilization.

 The very first **webcam** was invented at the University of Cambridge in 1991 solely to check remotely if the lab's coffee pot was empty, thus saving researchers unnecessary trips.

|| Internet is the decentralized infrastructure born in 1969 (ARPANET) and governed by TCP/IP since 1983, while the Web is the navigation interface created by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991. ||

Intro:
On **April 25, 1953**, the scientific journal Nature published a page-and-a-half article that would revolutionize our understanding of life. James Watson and Francis Crick described the **double helix** structure of DNA there.

[DNA double helix model Watson Crick]

This discovery, often described as the most important in modern biology, was not just a feat of molecular modeling. It was the culmination of decades of contradictory research and the Theater of one of the most famous ethical controversies in the history of sciences. Understanding the structure of DNA finally meant finding the physical mechanism allowing life to transmit itself, reproduce, and evolve.
Partie 1 Titre: The enigma of the carrier of heredity
Partie 1 Contenu:
Although **DNA** (deoxyribonucleic acid) was isolated for the first time in **1869** by <Friedrich Miescher>, its biological role remained an enigma for nearly eight decades. Most scientists thought that proteins, being more complex, carried genetic information. It was not until **1944** that Oswald Avery provided experimental proof that DNA is the true vector of heredity.

From there, a World-wide race began to decipher its shape, because in biology, function follows structure. In 1950, biochemist **Erwin Chargaff** established a fundamental rule: in any sample of DNA, the proportion of adenine (A) is equal to that of thymine (T), and that of guanine (G) equals that of cytosine (C). 

This observation, known as **Chargaff's Law**, suggested a specific Matching between these molecules, but no one had yet managed to visualize how these pieces fit together in three-dimensional space. James Watson and Francis Crick, working at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, tried to solve this puzzle by manipulating metal and cardboard models, without having direct experimental data themselves.

{Friedrich Miescher discovered DNA by analyzing the pus contained in used bandages from a nearby hospital: it was by isolating the nuclei of white blood cells that he found this new substance.}
Partie 2 Titre: Rosalind Franklin and the snapshot of truth
Partie 2 Contenu:
The key to the puzzle lay in London, at King's College, in the hands of **<Rosalind Franklin>**. An expert in <X-ray diffraction crystallography>, she succeeded in **1952** in obtaining images of unparalleled precision. The most famous, **"Photo 51"**, showed a characteristic cross unambiguously revealing a helical structure.

[Rosalind Franklin Photo 51 X-ray]

This is where history tips into controversy. In **January 1953**, Maurice Wilkins, a colleague of Franklin with whom she had a difficult relationship, showed this photo to James Watson without the researcher's permission. Seeing this image was a revelation for Watson: the precise measurements taken by Franklin (notably the periodicity of the helix and its diameter) confirmed that the two sugar-phosphate chains were on the outside, while the nitrogenous bases were turned toward the inside.

{If you unrolled all the DNA from a single human cell, it would measure about 2 meters. The human body contains 37 trillion cells, the equivalent of 70 billion km of DNA, which represents about 233 times the Earth-Sun round-trip distance.}

Using this "borrowed" data, Watson and Crick were able to finalize their model in just a few weeks, arranging the A-T and G-C pairs so that they fit perfectly in the center of the double helix.
Partie 3 Titre: The birth of molecular biology
Partie 3 Contenu:
Once the **double helix** structure was established, the scientific world immediately understood how life perpetuated itself. **<DNA replication>** became a mechanical evidence: the two strands of the helix separate like a zipper, and each strand serves as a template to build a new identical partner thanks to base complementarity.

This discovery opened the era of modern genetics, later allowing for <genome sequencing>, biotechnologies, and the understanding of genetic diseases. Watson and Crick had not just discovered a shape; they had discovered the universal language of life, a four-letter digital code (A, T, C, G) capable of storing prodigious amounts of information.

The scope of the 1953 article is all the more fascinating because of its extreme sobriety. The authors note with a touch of irony: "It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material." This discrete sentence announces the birth of a new discipline: molecular biology.
Partie 4 Titre: A legacy between glory and bitterness
Partie 4 Contenu:
The consecration came in **1962** when the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine** was awarded to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins. However, the name **<Rosalind Franklin>** was absent from the ceremony. Having passed away prematurely from ovarian cancer in **1958** at the age of 37, she could technically not receive the prize, as the Nobel statutes forbid posthumous awards.

However, beyond the legal impossibility, it is the lack of recognition during her lifetime that causes debate. In his book *The Double Helix* (1968), James Watson describes Franklin in an unflattering light, minimizing her scientific contribution. It would take decades for the international community to restore the historical truth: without Franklin's experimental rigor and technical expertise, Watson and Crick would probably never have completed their model before their American rival <Linus Pauling>.

Today, Rosalind Franklin has become an icon for women in science whose work was obscured or unfairly appropriated. Their legacy is celebrated in universities around the world, reminding us that science is a collective work where laboratory rigor is just as crucial as theoretical insight.

|| The double helix structure of DNA, published in 1953, explains the replication of life through base complementarity, but its success rests on the improperly used data of Rosalind Franklin. ||

Intro: Before the mid-19th century, entering an operating room was akin to passing through the gates of hell. The discovery of anesthesia in 1846 marks a fundamental break, not only technical but also moral, in the history of <sciences>. It transformed the perception of the suffering body and allowed for the rise of complex surgery, once unimaginable. This course explores the transition from "organized terror" to the birth of a rigorous medical discipline that revolutionized humanity's relationship with pain.
Partie 1 Titre: Surgery before anesthesia: a race against time
Partie 1 Contenu:
Before 1846, surgery was performed only as a last resort, in the face of certain death. The lack of pain control imposed a unique constraint on the practitioner: **speed**. A surgeon was not judged on his meticulousness, but on his ability to amputate a limb before the patient sank into a fatal **traumatic shock**. Operating rooms, often located at the top of buildings to benefit from natural light, were designed to isolate screams, while sturdy assistants held down struggling patients.

[surgery without anesthesia 19th century]

{The surgeon Robert Liston was so fast that he once accidentally amputated his assistant's fingers; both the patient and the assistant died of infection, and a spectator died of cardiac shock, making this the only operation in history with a 300% mortality rate.}

At that time, the only recourses were rudimentary sedatives like **alcohol**, **opium**, or **mesmerization** (a form of hypnosis), but none truly succeeded in suppressing the sensation of tearing tissues and bones. The profession of surgeon then required total psychological insensitivity, an "iron hand" capable of ignoring the pleas of the patient. This physiological limit blocked all medical progress: it was impossible to open the abdomen or the thorax on a conscious and agitated patient.
Partie 2 Titre: Ether Day: the Boston shift (1846)
Partie 2 Contenu:
On **October 16, 1846**, at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, an experiment definitely changed the course of History. The dentist **<William Morton>**, who had long been looking for a way to extract teeth without pain, organized a public demonstration. He used an inhaler of his invention containing **sulfuric ether**, whose intoxicating properties were known recreationally but never successfully applied to major surgery.

[ether anesthesia first demonstration 1846]

{Before becoming a medical tool, ether was used in student parties called "Ether frolics", where guests inhaled the gas to laugh and stagger, not realizing they no longer felt the blows they gave themselves when falling.}

Before the eyes of an amphitheater filled with skeptical students and doctors, Morton administered the gas to **Gilbert Abbott**. Once the patient was asleep, the surgeon **John Warren** proceeded to excise a vascular tumor in the neck. Unlike the usual scenes of torture, the patient remained still, his breathing calm. Upon Abbott's awakening, who confirmed feeling nothing, Warren declared to the assembly: "Gentlemen, this is no humbug."

This success marks the end of systematic surgical pain. The news crossed the Atlantic in record time. As early as December 1846, Robert Liston himself performed the first amputation under ether in London, exclaiming that this "Yankee dodge" beat everything he had ever known. However, this revolution was not welcomed without friction: some clergy opposed anesthesia, arguing that pain was a necessary divine trial, particularly during childbirth.
Partie 3 Titre: Patent wars and chemical evolution
Partie 3 Contenu:
The success of ether immediately triggered a violent battle for the priority of the invention. **Crawford Long**, a country doctor, claimed to have used ether as early as **1842**, but his lack of publication deprived him of World recognition. Meanwhile, **Charles Jackson**, a chemist, claimed to be the real brain behind Morton's idea. This quarrel ended up poisoning the lives of the protagonists, with Morton dying ruined by endless lawsuits to validate his patent.

On a technical level, ether had major drawbacks: it was irritating to the respiratory tract and highly flammable. In 1847, the Scottish obstetrician **James Young Simpson** introduced **chloroform**. More powerful and more pleasantly scented, it quickly became the favorite product in Europe.

{James Young Simpson discovered the virtues of chloroform during a dinner with friends: after inhaling some to test the product, they all woke up the next morning under the dining room table, thus proving the radical effectiveness of the gas.}

Its use was definitively legitimized in 1853 when **Queen Victoria** accepted it for the birth of her eighth child, silencing the last religious objections.

Over the decades, chemical research led to the discovery of less toxic and more precise agents. Medicine then moved from a brutal sleep-inducing technique to a fine management of the state of consciousness, opening the way for modern long-duration surgery.
Partie 4 Titre: The birth of a specialty: anesthesiology
Partie 4 Contenu:
The discovery of anesthetic gases was only a first step. At the end of the 19th century, the understanding of microorganisms thanks to <Antisepsie (Semmelweis and Lister)> completed the medical arsenal: one could now operate without pain AND without infection. Anesthesia then became a science of monitoring. One no longer merely put the patient to sleep; one learned to monitor their **vital signs** (pulse, breathing).

{The word "anesthesia" was suggested to William Morton by the poet and physician Oliver Wendell Holmes, from the Ancient Greek meaning "absence of sensation"; before that, it was simply called "gaseous preparation".}

The 20th century saw the appearance of **intravenous anesthesia** and muscle relaxants, which allowed for the relaxation of muscles without the need to administer massive and dangerous doses of gas. Today, the anesthesiologist is an indispensable pillar of the operating room. They precisely dose analgesia (pain suppression), narcosis (sleep), and muscle relaxation, ensuring the safety of the patient during interventions that can last more than twelve hours.

Surgery has thus moved from a spectacle of brutal speed to a discipline of surgical precision. Without anesthesia, organ transplants, cardiac surgery, or neurosurgery could never have seen the light of day. It is one of the rare fields where science has succeeded in abolishing a multi-millennial biological fatality.

Intro: In 1859, the publication of **"On the Origin of Species"** by **Charles Darwin** marked a major epistemological break. This text did not just propose that species change over time, an idea already in the making among some naturalists; it offered for the first time a universal, rational, and verifiable explanatory mechanism: **<natural selection>**. By unifying all of the life sciences under a single biological law, Darwin moved humanity from its providential pedestal to place it within an immense common lineage. This course explores the genesis of this revolution, from the deck of the Beagle to the foundations of modern biology.
Partie 1 Titre: The awakening of a naturalist: the voyage of the Beagle
Partie 1 Contenu:
In December **1831**, the young **Charles Darwin** embarked on an expedition around the world aboard the **<HMS Beagle>**. His initial mission was cartographic, but the trip quickly transformed into an immense enterprise of collecting geological and biological specimens. During five years of travel, Darwin amassed observations that contradicted the fixist vision of the time, according to which species were created once and for all in their current form.

[Charles Darwin portrait]

It was during his stopover in the **Galápagos Islands** in 1835 that the most famous click in the history of biology occurred. He observed varieties of **<finches>** that were morphologically close, but whose beak shapes varied radically from one island to another. This specialization seemed directly linked to the available food resources: strong beaks for cracking seeds, or thin ones for capturing insects.

[Darwin finches Galapagos beaks]

Darwin then began to doubt the immutability of species. He sensed that these birds shared a common ancestor from the mainland and that they had modified over time to adapt to their respective environments. Back in England in 1836, he would nevertheless take more than **20 years** to formalize his intuitions, aware that his theory would shake the religious and social foundations of Victorian society.

{The captain of the Beagle, Robert FitzRoy, was a fervent creationist who bitterly regretted all his life having involuntarily allowed Darwin to gather the evidence for his theory.}
Partie 2 Titre: Natural selection: life's algorithm
Partie 2 Contenu:
To structure his thinking, Darwin relied on four implacable logical pillars. The first is **variation**: within a population, all individuals are slightly different. The second is **selection pressure**: the natural environment cannot support the infinite expansion of populations, creating a struggle for survival. 

The third pillar is **adaptive advantage**: in this competitive environment, certain biological traits (running faster, better resisting cold, having a beak adapted to hard seeds) increase the chances of survival and reproduction. Finally, **hereditary transmission** ensures that these advantageous traits propagate from generation to generation.

This process, which Darwin calls **natural selection**, is a blind mechanism, without intention or final goal. Contrary to popular belief, it is not the victory of the strongest, but the survival of the best adapted. Through the accumulation of these micro-changes over millions of years, entire populations are transformed, eventually forming new species. This is what Darwin calls **descent with modification**, drawing the image of a tree of life where all creatures are connected by common ancestors.
Partie 3 Titre: The clash of ideas and the decisive role of Wallace
Partie 3 Contenu:
Despite the solidity of his work, Darwin hesitated to publish, fearing public disgrace. Everything changed in **1858** when he received a manuscript from a young naturalist exploring Malaysia, **<Alfred Russel Wallace>**. To Darwin's astonishment, Wallace had, independently, reached the same conclusions about natural selection. Under pressure from his scientific friends, Darwin rushed the writing of his masterpiece so as not to lose the priority of his discovery.

The public reaction was violent. The most radical implication of the theory, although Darwin was careful not to make it explicit in his first work, was that the human being is just one animal among others, coming from the same lineage as the great apes. This idea provoked epic debates, like the one in 1860 between Bishop **<Samuel Wilberforce>** and biologist **<Thomas Huxley>**, nicknamed "Darwin's bulldog" for his fierce defense of the theory.

Huxley then embodied the transition of science from shadow to light, refusing to let religious dogmas dictate biological truth. Darwin's theory gradually imposed itself not through ideological fervor, but through its unmatched ability to explain the natural world with an economy of means and a scientific precision never before achieved.
Partie 4 Titre: The legacy: from Darwinism to modern genetics
Partie 4 Contenu:
Darwin knew nothing of the mechanisms of heredity. He did not know how traits were physically transmitted from parents to children. It would take until the 20th century for the discovery of **<DNA>** and work on **genetics** to fill this void. This fusion between natural selection and genetics is today called the **modern synthesis**. 

Far from being a simple hypothesis, evolution is a fact observed daily. It can be seen in the resistance of bacteria to antibiotics or in the rapid evolution of certain viruses. Darwin's theory transformed biology, once a simple science of cataloging, into a predictive and dynamic science. It teaches us that life is in perpetual flux and that today's biodiversity is the result of a story four billion years long.

|| Darwin revolutionized our vision of the world in 1859 by demonstrating that the complexity of life emerges from a natural and blind process: natural selection. ||

{The expression "survival of the fittest" was coined by philosopher Herbert Spencer to justify social inequalities, a concept that Darwin himself found scientifically dubious.}

Intro:
**13.8 billion years** ago, the entire universe - all matter, all energy, and space itself - was concentrated in a state of extreme density and temperature. This initial state, which scientists call a <singularity>, marks the beginning of cosmic history.

[Big Bang universe expansion galaxies]

Contrary to a common misconception, the Big Bang does not refer to a single moment of creation, but the cosmological model describing the evolution of the universe since that primordial moment. In a fraction of a second, it began to expand at a dazzling rate. This expansion continues today, continuously shaping the structure of the cosmos and pushing galaxies away from each other.
Partie 1 Titre: Deconstructing the explosion myth
Partie 1 Contenu:
The term **"Big Bang"** is one of the most famous in science, but also one of the most misunderstood. One should not imagine this Event as an explosion of matter spreading into a pre-existing vacuum. In reality, it is space itself that is stretching. Before this moment, there was neither space, nor time, nor matter as we know them. The question "what was there before?" is often considered to be without physical meaning, because time began with this Event.

The origin of the name is paradoxical. The term was coined in **1949** by the British astrophysicist **Fred Hoyle**. Ironically, Hoyle was a fierce opponent of this Theory: he defended the steady-state model, according to which the universe had always existed without major change. By using the expression "Big Bang" during a BBC broadcast, he sought to ridicule the idea of a sudden beginning. Although Hoyle was wrong on the substance, his vivid expression caught the public imagination and remained the official name.

This expansion has no "center". If you imagine the surface of a balloon being inflated, every point moves away from the others without a single point on the surface being designated as the middle of the expansion. This is precisely what happens in our three-dimensional universe.

 Despite his opposition to the Big Bang, Fred Hoyle discovered how stars manufacture complex chemical elements (carbon, oxygen) through nuclear fusion, which would have earned him the Nobel Prize had he not been so controversial.
Partie 2 Titre: The pillars of observational evidence
Partie 2 Contenu:
Sciences do not rely on simple suppositions, but on tangible evidence. The first major breakthrough dates back to **1929**, when the astronomer **Edwin Hubble** observed the Movement of distant galaxies. He noticed a systematic phenomenon: the further a galaxy is from Earth, the faster it seems to move away. This proportional link between distance and speed, called Hubble's constant, proves that the universe is not static but in full expansion.

[Hubble deep field galaxies]

The second major proof, and arguably the most spectacular, is the **<cosmic microwave background>**. In **1965**, two engineers, **Arno Penzias** and **Robert Wilson**, working on a telecommunication antenna, picked up a constant background noise, a sleet that came from everywhere at once. After eliminating all possible terrestrial sources, they realized they had just detected the thermal "echo" of the Big Bang. This microwave radiation was emitted 380,000 years after the start of the universe, at the precise moment when light was able to circulate freely for the first time.

 A small part of the "snow" or sleet that you could see on old un-tuned analog televisions comes directly from this cosmic microwave background.

Finally, the abundance of light elements confirms the model. Calculations predict that the first minutes of the Big Bang must have produced about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium. Telescopic observations show exactly these proportions in the oldest gas clouds in the universe, thus validating the Theory of <primordial nucleosynthesis>.
Partie 3 Titre: The chronology of origins
Partie 3 Contenu:
Modern physics allows us to go back in time with dizzying precision, but it hits an invisible wall: the **Planck Time**, located at **10⁻⁴³ seconds** after the initial instant. Before this threshold, temperature and density are so high that our current laws (general Relativity and quantum physics) are no longer compatible. This is the realm of the unknown.

Just after, the universe goes through a phase of **Inflation**, an exponential expansion in a fraction of a second that makes the universe homogeneous. At **3 minutes**, the temperature drops enough for protons and neutrons to assemble: this is the birth of the first atomic nuclei. However, the universe remains an opaque fog of free electrons that block light.

It takes **380,000 years** for "recombination" to occur: electrons are captured by nuclei to form the first neutral atoms. Light is finally released: it is the emission of the **<cosmic microwave background>**. As for the first **stars**, they only appear about **200 million years** later, ending the "dark ages". Our own solar system is a newcomer, formed only **4.6 billion years** ago, benefiting from matter recycled by generations of long-gone stars.

 If the 13.8-billion-year History of the universe were scaled down to a single calendar year, the Big Bang would take place on January 1st at midnight and the human species would only make its appearance on December 31st at 11:52 PM.
Partie 4 Titre: The future and accelerated expansion
Partie 4 Contenu:
For a long time, cosmologists wondered if gravity would eventually stop the expansion to cause a final collapse. However, a major discovery in **1998** overturned this vision: the **<accelerated expansion of the universe>**. By observing distant <supernovae>, researchers realized that the universe is not just expanding, but doing so faster and faster.

This mysterious force pushing the universe apart is called **dark energy**. It would represent about 68% of the total content of the universe, while ordinary matter (what we are made of) accounts for only 5%. This acceleration suggests that the universe will end in a state of absolute cold and total dilution, a scenario named the **Big Freeze**.

The observable universe, which is the part of space that light has had time to travel to reach us, has a radius of about **46 billion light-years**. This figure exceeds 13.8 billion years because, while the light was traveling towards us, the space between it and us continued to stretch. This immensity reminds us that we are seeing only a tiny fraction of a whole that could well be infinite.

|| The Big Bang, which occurred 13.8 billion years ago, is not an explosion in space but the expansion of space itself, proven by the receding of galaxies and fossil radiation. ||

Intro:
A volcano is not a simple mountain spitting fire, but a window open onto the thermal and chemical activity of our planet. It is a rupture in the outer structure of the Earth through which magma, a complex mixture of molten rock and gases under high pressure, rises to the surface to become lava.

Understanding this phenomenon requires exploring the depths of the lithosphere and analyzing the titanic forces that drive the heart of the globe to maintain its thermal balance.

[volcano eruption lava]
Partie 1 Titre: The dynamics of the Earth's depths
Partie 1 Contenu:
The Earth is not an inert block of rock, but a stack of layers with distinct physical properties. The surface layer, the **crust**, is a rigid shell whose thickness varies from **5 to 70 km**. Below lies the **mantle**, a colossal structure reaching down to **2,900 km** in depth. Although composed of solid rocks (notably peridotite), the mantle behaves in a ductile manner over geological timescales, allowing for the circulation of matter.

This circulation is governed by **convection currents**. Intense heat from the decay of radioactive elements in the Earth's core heats the rocks of the deep mantle. Having become less dense, these rocks slowly rise toward the surface, cool down, then sink back. This cyclic Movement acts as a conveyor belt for <tectonic plates>, causing them to collide or move apart.

It is at the boundaries of these plates that most geological activity is concentrated. When plates move apart at the level of <mid-ocean ridges>, pressure drops sharply, favoring the partial melting of rocks. Conversely, during <subduction>, one plate sinks beneath another, dragging with it sediments and water that modify the mantle's chemistry.

{Some very deep eruptions bring up pieces of the mantle so quickly that they don't have time to transform: this is how diamonds, formed more than 150 km deep, reach the surface intact.}
Partie 2 Titre: The genesis of magma and its ascent
Partie 2 Contenu:
The **magma** results from the partial melting of mantle or crustal rocks. Contrary to popular belief, rock does not melt solely because it is "hot". Geologists identify three triggers: an **increase in temperature**, a **decrease in pressure** (adiabatic melting), or the **addition of water**. Water acts as a chemical flux, lowering the melting point of surrounding rocks, a crucial process in <subduction> zones.

Once formed, magma is less dense than the surrounding solid rock. It then begins an ascent through failures in the lithosphere, driven by buoyancy. This journey toward the surface is often interrupted in **magma chambers**. These reservoirs located a few kilometers deep serve as storage and chemical differentiation zones.

In these chambers, pressure builds up critically. Gases dissolved in the mixture (water vapor, carbon dioxide) begin to form bubbles as the magma rises, like a carbonated drink being opened. If the cap rock can no longer contain this internal energy, the eruption is triggered.

{The eruption of Tambora in 1815 was so powerful that it cooled the global climate, causing "the year without a summer" in 1816. Catastrophic harvests in Europe and North America led to the worst famine of the 19th century.}
Partie 3 Titre: Viscosity and eruptive styles
Partie 3 Contenu:
Not all eruptions look the same; their violence depends directly on the **viscosity of the magma**, which is itself Dicté by its silica content. A magma low in silica (basaltic) is very fluid. It allows gases to escape without resistance, producing **effusive eruptions**. This is the case with Piton de la Fournaise or the volcanoes of **Hawaii**, where lava flows quietly, forming broad shield volcanoes.

In contrast, magmas rich in silica are extremely viscous. Gases remain trapped until the pressure becomes unbearable. The resulting explosion is devastating, projecting ash and <pyroclastic flows>. These **explosive eruptions** are characteristic of Ring of Fire volcanoes, such as **Pinatubo** or Mount **St Helens**.

Volcanoes can also remain "dormant" for millennia before waking up abruptly. The most famous case is that of **Vesuvius** in 79 AD, which buried Pompeii under meters of ash. The record for power, however, goes to **Tambora** in 1815, whose explosion was heard more than 2,000 km away.

|| Volcanoes form where tectonic plates separate or collide - 80% of the world's volcanic activity happens under the oceans.||
Partie 4 Titre: Planetary impact and geological legacy
Partie 4 Contenu:
Volcanism is not just a natural hazard; it is an essential engine of Earth's evolution. Over the long term, volcanoes are the primary architects of the primitive atmosphere through the degassing of volatile compounds. Even today, volcanic ash, rich in minerals, creates exceptionally fertile agricultural lands that attract large populations despite the danger.

However, major eruptions can temporarily modify the solar cycle. Sulfur aerosols projected into the **Stratosphere** reflect sunlight, causing global cooling. This phenomenon generated the "**year without a summer**" following the Tambora episode. Furthermore, certain sites like the Yellowstone <supervolcano> are under constant monitoring, as an eruption at this scale would have systemic planetary consequences.

Finally, underwater volcanism plays a key role in the chemical regulation of the oceans. The <black smokers>, hydrothermal vents located near mid-ocean ridges, host unique ecosystems based on **chemosynthesis** rather than photosynthesis, proving that Earth's geothermal energy can suffice to support life in the total darkness of the abyss.

{The largest known volcano in the solar system is not on Earth but on Mars: Olympus Mons rises 22 km high, nearly three times Everest, because the absence of plate tectonics allowed magma to accumulate in the same Place for millions of years.}

|| TO REMEMBER: Volcanoes expel magma accumulated under pressure in magma chambers, under the influence of tectonic movements and the viscosity of molten rocks. ||

Intro:
Every year, the Earth records about **500,000 detectable earthquakes**, a few dozen of which are powerful enough to reshape landscapes and cause major structural damage.

[earthquake collapsed buildings urban]

An earthquake is not a random Event, but the brutal conclusion of a long process of energy accumulation. Understanding earthquakes requires exploring the dynamic structure of our planet, from continental drift to the microscopic physics of rock failure under pressure.
Partie 1 Titre: Plate tectonics: the framework of terrestrial dynamics
Partie 1 Contenu:
The Earth's surface is not a rigid and immobile shell; it is divided into a dozen major **tectonic plates** that float on the asthenosphere, a layer of the Earth's mantle with ductile properties. These plates move at a speed of **1 to 10 cm per year**, which corresponds approximately to the growth speed of human fingernails.

[tectonic plates collision]

These movements are governed by convection currents from the internal heat of the Earth. Plates interact primarily at their boundaries in three different ways. In divergence zones, such as mid-ocean ridges, they move apart to make room for new magma. In convergence zones, they collide, often causing **subduction** (one plate dives beneath another) or the formation of mountains.

Finally, they can slide laterally against each other along transform faults, like the famous <San Andreas> in California. It is precisely at these junctions that the vast majority of the world's earthquakes are concentrated, because the fluid Movement of the plates is hindered by the roughness of the Earth's crust.

{If tectonic plates suddenly stopped moving, the Earth would lose its magnetic protection over time, because the Movement of plates is linked to the dissipation of heat from the core which generates our magnetosphere.}
Partie 2 Titre: Fault mechanics and elastic accumulation
Partie 2 Contenu:
An earthquake occurs along a **fault**, a fracture that separates two rock blocks. In Theory, the Movement of tectonic plates should drive these blocks continuously. However, due to the roughness of the rock surfaces, **friction** is stronger than the force of the Movement. The blocks then stay stuck against each other.

[San Andreas fault aerial view]

Despite this apparent blockage, the tectonic plates continue to push. The rock, although rigid, possesses a certain elasticity. It then deforms slowly, accumulating what sciences call **elastic stress**, much like a bow being pulled tighter and tighter. This preparation stage can last for decades, even centuries.

The rupture threshold is reached when the accumulated energy exceeds the resistance of the fault rocks.
