The blockage then suddenly gives way: the two blocks slide against each other in a few milliseconds. This elastic relaxation instantly releases the stored energy in the form of **seismic waves**. The precise point of the rupture at depth is the **focus**, while at the surface, the impact is maximal at the **epicenter**.
Partie 3 Titre: Moment magnitude and collateral hazards
Partie 3 Contenu:
To measure the power of an earthquake, seismologists use the **moment <magnitude scale>** (Mw), which has largely replaced the Richter scale for major events. This measurement is a logarithmic function: a 1-point increase on the scale multiplies the energy released by approximately **32**.

To Date, the most powerful earthquake ever recorded with modern instruments is the **Valdivia earthquake in Chile (1960)**, reaching a magnitude of **9.5**. Such an Event releases energy comparable to thousands of atomic bombs.

When the focus of a powerful earthquake is located under the ocean, the vertical movement of the seafloor suddenly displaces an immense column of water, generating a **tsunami**. These waves, initially imperceptible in the high seas because they are very long, rise violently as they approach the coasts.

The **Indian Ocean tsunami (2004)** illustrates the global reach of this phenomenon: triggered by a magnitude 9.1 earthquake near Sumatra, it traveled thousands of kilometers to strike 14 countries, causing the death of **227,000 people**. This highlights that the danger of an earthquake does not stop at the immediate ground shaking.

{Contrary to a popular belief, a magnitude 0 or negative earthquake exists: the scale is open and measures micro-earthquakes so weak that they are only detectable by ultra-sensitive sensors placed in a laboratory.}
Partie 4 Titre: Wave propagation and urban resilience
Partie 4 Contenu:
Once the fault has ruptured, energy travels through the Earth via different types of waves. The first to arrive are **P-waves** (primary), which compress the rock like an accordion. They are followed by **S-waves** (secondary), which are slower and more destructive, making the ground oscillate perpendicularly to their direction. Finally, surface waves are those that cause the most visible damage to buildings.

Modern sciences do not yet allow the prediction of the exact Date of an earthquake, but they can identify risk zones thanks to fault mapping. Prevention therefore relies on **earthquake engineering**. In countries like Japan, skyscrapers are equipped with **seismic isolators** (Giants shock absorbers or foundations on bearings) that allow the structure to dissipate energy instead of absorbing it.

Educating populations and setting up early warning systems - capable of detecting P-waves and cutting gas networks or stopping trains before the arrival of more destructive S-waves - save thousands of lives every year. Earthquake resilience is as much a matter of geology as it is of technological and social preparation.

|| To remember: Earthquakes arise from the brutal rupture of rocks that have accumulated centuries of elastic stress at the boundaries of tectonic plates. This energy propagates in the form of waves, whose magnitude follows a logarithmic scale where each unit multiplies the energy released by 32. ||

Intro:
On **April 26, 1986**, at 1:23 AM, reactor No. 4 of the **Chernobyl** nuclear power plant in Soviet Ukraine was the scene of the most serious industrial accident of the modern era. This disaster, ranked at level 7 (the highest) on the **INES** scale, released into the atmosphere a quantity of radioactive particles estimated at **400 times more radioactivity** than the Hiroshima bomb. Beyond the immediate human drama, this Event permanently altered our relationship with atomic energy and acted as an accelerator for the fall of the Soviet Union.

[Chernobyl nuclear plant 1986 explosion]
Partie 1 Titre: The fatal spiral: a human and technical failure
Partie 1 Contenu:
The tragedy originated in a safety test paradoxically meant to improve the resilience of the plant. Engineers wanted to verify if, in the event of a power cut, the **Inertia** of the spinning turbines could provide enough energy to power the cooling pumps during the 40 seconds required to start the emergency diesel generators.

However, a series of delays and administrative pressures pushed the night shift to perform the test under low-power conditions, making the reactor unstable. The core of the reactor, a <Soviet RBMK reactor> type, possessed a dangerous physical characteristic: a **positive void coefficient**. This means that if steam bubbles form in the cooling circuit, the nuclear reaction accelerates instead of slowing down.

When at 1:23:40 AM, the operator activated the **AZ-5** emergency shutdown button, the graphite control rods, supposed to stop the reaction, caused a massive initial power surge due to their defective design. In a fraction of a second, power rose to **30,000%** of its nominal value. The steam pressure then pulverized the **1,000-ton** upper biological shield, exposing the melting core to the open air and projecting highly radioactive debris for kilometers around.

{The reactor burned at such a temperature that it created a corium magma, a nuclear lava nicknamed 'the Elephant's Foot' because of its shape; staying 300 seconds in contact with it in 1986 was fatal in less than two days.}
Partie 2 Titre: Denial and the sacrifice of the liquidators
Partie 2 Contenu:
In the hours following the explosion, the Soviet state apparatus sank into denial. The first **firefighters** dispatched to the scene fought what they believed to be a simple roof fire. Without protective equipment, they handled blocks of **graphite** with their bare hands, unaware that these debris were the very components of the reactor core. Within hours, the first symptoms of **acute radiation syndrome** (nausea, skin burns) appeared.

As radiation sensors went off the charts, official reports minimized the scale of the disaster. The nearby city of **Pripyat**, built for the plant workers, continued its normal life for 36 hours. Children played outside under a rain of invisible ash, while authorities waited for Moscow's approval to act. It was not until the afternoon of April 27 that the 50,000 inhabitants were evacuated in a few hours, leaving behind an entire life.

To extinguish the fire and seal the reactor, the USSR mobilized nearly 600,000 people: the <liquidators>. Among them, helicopter pilots dropped sand and lead onto the gaping core, while soldiers, nicknamed **biological robots**, had a maximum of 90 seconds to clear debris on the roof of the adjacent reactor, as electronic machines failed under the effect of extreme radiation.

[Pripyat abandoned city Chernobyl]

{Some liquidators received a medal showing a drop of blood crossed by alpha, beta, and gamma rays; it is one of the rare military decorations in the world created to reward sacrifice against an invisible enemy.}
Partie 3 Titre: Health and environmental impacts: between myths and realities
Partie 3 Contenu:
The consequences of Chernobyl are the subject of intense scientific debate. The radioactive cloud, carried by the winds, crossed Europe as far as France and Scandinavia, depositing **cesium-137** and **iodine-131** on the ground. On the health front, the WHO recognizes about **4,000 cases of thyroid cancer**, mainly in children who consumed contaminated milk. However, the total toll of indirect deaths (future cancers, stress-related diseases) varies according to studies from a few thousand to several tens of thousands.

At the center of the disaster, a <30 km exclusion zone> today offers a striking spectacle. The absence of human activity has transformed this contaminated territory into an open-air laboratory. Contrary to expectations, nature is not dead there: without the pressure of agriculture and urbanization, populations of wolves, elk, and Przewalski's horses are more numerous than before the disaster. The radioactivity induces local genetic mutations, but it turns out to be less deleterious for the survival of species than human presence was.

On a technical level, a first concrete **sarcophagus** was built in haste in 1986 to isolate the reactor. Weakened by time, it was covered in 2016 by the **New Safe Confinement**. This monumental steel structure, designed to last 100 years, was assembled at a distance and then slid on rails to avoid exposing workers to residual radiation from the site.
Partie 4 Titre: The legacy of a global disaster
Partie 4 Contenu:
Chernobyl is not just a technical accident; it is a geopolitical earthquake. For <Mikhail Gorbachev>, then leader of the USSR, the disaster revealed the systemic flaws of the Soviet Union: bureaucratic secrecy, industrial obsolescence, and disregard for human safety. The Event forced the implementation of **Glasnost** (policy of transparency), indirectly precipitating the fall of the Eastern Bloc.

On a global scale, the accident shattered the myth of infallible nuclear energy. It led to the creation of the **World Association of Nuclear Operators** (<WANO>) to promote the exchange of best practices between countries and prevent such a tragedy from happening again. Many Western countries, following 1986, froze their nuclear programs or accelerated the transition to other energy sources.

The accident remains today an absolute reference in risk management and the psychology of disasters. It reminds us that technological power requires political transparency and flawless scientific rigor so as not to turn against its creators.

|| Chernobyl (1986) released 400 times more radioactivity than Hiroshima - the <30 km exclusion zone> remains uninhabited by man, but wildlife paradoxically thrives there. ||

Titre: Why doesn't the Moon fall onto Earth?
Intro:
Why doesn't the Moon crash into us even though Earth's gravity attracts it irresistibly? The short answer is paradoxical: the Moon is indeed "falling" toward Earth continuously, but it systematically misses it at every moment.

[Moon Earth orbit space]

This dynamic, which defines the very Concept of an orbit, constitutes one of the pillars of classical mechanics. Understanding this fragile balance between free fall and Movement of Inertia means diving into the physics of **Isaac Newton**, who was the first to unify the laws of falling bodies on Earth with those of the Movement of celestial bodies in the sky.

{If you weighed 60 kg on Earth, you would only weigh 10 on the Moon, as its gravity is six times weaker than ours.}
Partie 1 Titre: The metaphor of Newton's cannon
Partie 1 Contenu:
To make a then-revolutionary Concept accessible, **Isaac Newton** imagined a now-famous thought experiment: a cannon located at the top of a mountain so high that it would exit Earth's atmosphere to free itself from air resistance.

[Newton cannonball orbit thought experiment]

If a ball is fired horizontally with little power, gravity pulls it toward the ground and it describes a quick curve before crashing. If the powder charge is increased, the ball travels a longer distance. However, if a specific velocity is reached, called **Orbital velocity**, a remarkable phenomenon occurs: as the ball falls toward the ground, the surface of the Earth, which is round, curves and drops away beneath it at the same speed.

The projectile then finds itself in a state of perpetual **free fall**. It falls without ever hitting the ground, because its curved trajectory perfectly matches the roundness of the planet. This is precisely the state of the Moon: it possesses enough lateral velocity to transform what should be an impact into an infinite loop.

{Newton's original 1687 manuscript shows a diagram almost identical to those used today by NASA to explain the orbiting of satellites.}
Partie 2 Titre: The balance of forces involved
Partie 2 Contenu:
The Moon currently orbits at an average distance of **384,000 km**. To maintain this balance, its lateral displacement speed is approximately **1 km/s**. This speed is the rampart that prevents it from succumbing to gravitational attraction.

If the Moon stopped dead in its tracks, it would fall vertically and crash into the Earth in a few days. Conversely, if Earth's gravity vanished instantly, the Moon would escape in a straight line into the interstellar void, in accordance with the principle of Inertia. The orbit is therefore the result of a permanent compromise between these two tendencies.

<Newton's universal gravitation> Law teaches us that the force of this attraction depends on the mass of the objects and the distance separating them. The closer a satellite is to Earth, the stronger the attraction, and the higher its speed must be to avoid falling. This is why the **International Space Station** (ISS), located only 400 km up, must fly at **7.7 km/s** (about 28,000 km/h) to stay in orbit, completing a trip around the World in just 90 minutes compared to 27.3 days for the Moon.

This difference illustrates the decrease in gravitational influence with distance, a key Concept for understanding why celestial objects do not all instantly clump together.
Partie 3 Titre: The influence of tides and distancing
Partie 3 Contenu:
Contrary to popular belief, the lunar orbit is not a fixed system. It is subject to the influence of <tidal forces>. The Moon's gravity deforms Earth's oceans, creating a "bulge" of water. Since the Earth rotates on its axis faster than the Moon orbits it, this bulge slightly leads the Moon's position.

This shift creates friction that slows Earth's rotation: our days lengthen by about 1.4 milliseconds per century. In return, through a transfer of kinetic energy, the Moon recovers this lost energy and moves away from us. The calculation is precise: our satellite moves away from the Earth by **3.8 cm per year**.

This process has major historical and biological consequences. Several billion years ago, the Moon was much closer, perhaps only 25,000 km away. Tides were then titanic walls of water crashing several times a day on primordial coasts, accelerating erosion and the chemical mixing necessary for the appearance of life.

{Due to this slowing of the Earth, dinosaurs lived on a planet where days lasted only 22 or 23 hours.}
Partie 4 Titre: A future without total eclipses
Partie 4 Contenu:
The progressive distancing of the Moon means that the current configuration of the sky is exceptional. Today, by a fascinating geometric coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times larger than the Moon, but also 400 times further away. This allows the two stars to have the same apparent size in the sky and makes total solar eclipses possible.

However, in about **600 million years**, the Moon will have become so distant that it will appear too small to totally mask the solar disk. Future inhabitants of the Earth (if any remain) will only be able to observe annular eclipses, where a ring of light surrounds the lunar silhouette.

In the very long term, one could imagine the Moon eventually escaping, but this is not the most likely scenario. In about **50 billion years**, Earth's rotation will be synchronized with the lunar orbit: the Earth will always show the same face to the Moon, just as the Moon already always shows us the same face. The system will then be stabilized, unless the Sun destroys the Earth long before during its red giant phase.

{During its red giant phase, the Sun will swell so much that it could swallow Mercury and Venus, and its edge could graze Earth's orbit.}

|| The Moon does not crash because its lateral velocity exactly counterbalances Earth's attraction, creating a perpetual free fall that paradoxically moves it 3.8 cm away per year. ||

Titre: Is there life elsewhere in the Universe?
Intro:
The immensity of the cosmos defies human imagination: the observable universe contains approximately **2,000 billion galaxies**, each home to hundreds of billions of stars. If we apply simple statistical logic, the number of potentially habitable planets numbers in the trillions. Yet, despite this theoretical profusion, we have faced a total radio silence since the dawn of modern astronomy.

[radio telescope SETI]

This apparent contradiction between the high probability of the existence of extraterrestrial civilizations and the total absence of evidence or contact is known as the **Fermi paradox**. This line of questioning is no longer just a matter of science fiction, but a rigorous scientific discipline: **Exobiology**.
Partie 1 Titre: The chemistry of life and the planetary cradle
Partie 1 Contenu:
To search for life elsewhere, scientists first rely on the only known model: terrestrial life. This is based on two fundamental pillars: **carbon chemistry**, capable of forming complex organic molecules, and **liquid water**, which serves as an essential solvent for biological reactions.

The first criterion for a planet to be a candidate for life is its orbital position. It must be located within the **<habitable zone>** of its star. This is a region where the energy flux received allows for the maintenance of a surface temperature compatible with the presence of liquid water. If the planet is too close, the greenhouse effect spirals out of control and the water evaporates; if it is too far away, the water freezes permanently.

Since the **discovery of exoplanets** (planets orbiting stars other than the Sun) in the 1990s, our vision has changed. We now know of more than **5,500**, and the data suggests that almost every star in our galaxy has at least one planet. However, habitability does not mean the presence of life: other factors such as the presence of a protective atmosphere or a magnetic field are crucial.

{There are more stars in the observable universe than there are grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth. Statistically, even a one-in-a-billion probability of life appearing would imply millions of biological centers just in our galaxy.}

To conceptualize this probability, astronomer **Frank Drake** proposed the **<Drake equation>** in 1961. This formula attempts to estimate the number of technologically advanced civilizations in the Milky Way by multiplying various factors (rate of star formation, fraction of habitable planets, probability of the emergence of intelligence). Although unverifiable, it structures the scientific debate.
Partie 2 Titre: The unsuspected oases of the solar system
Partie 2 Contenu:
There is no need to look toward distant stars to find fascinating environments. Within our own solar system, celestial bodies challenge the idea that life can only exist on a temperate rocky planet. Research is now focusing on the moons of the gas giants.

**Europa**, one of the satellites of Jupiter, is the most serious candidate. Beneath an ice crust several kilometers thick hides a global **liquid water ocean**. This ocean is kept liquid not by the Sun, which is too distant, but by **<tidal forces>**: the colossal gravitational pull of Jupiter deforms the moon, creating internal friction that generates heat.

[Europa moon Jupiter ice ocean]

**Enceladus**, a small moon of Saturn, presents an even more spectacular phenomenon: it ejects geysers of water vapor and organic particles through cracks at its south pole. The **Cassini** probe was able to fly through these plumes and detect silicates and molecular hydrogen, probable signs of hydrothermal activity at the bottom of its ocean. This suggests the existence of chemical energy sources capable of nourishing microbial life without any sunlight.

Finally, **Mars** remains a major subject of study. We know that liquid water once flowed on its surface. Today, robotic explorers are looking for **<biosignatures>** (fossil or chemical traces) proving that life could have appeared there before the planet lost its atmosphere and most of its water.
Partie 3 Titre: The Fermi paradox or the enigma of silence
Partie 3 Contenu:
In 1950, the physicist **Enrico Fermi** raised a question during an informal lunch: if advanced civilizations exist by the thousands, why do we see no trace of them? This is the heart of the paradox: the universe is old (13.8 billion years); a civilization just one million years ahead of us would have had ample time to colonize the galaxy, even at sub-luminal speeds.

Several hypotheses attempt to resolve this "Great Silence." The first is that of the **<Great Filter>**: there would be a stage in evolution (the transition from simple to complex cell, or the invention of self-destructive technologies like the atom) that is almost impossible to clear. Either we have already passed this filter (we are an exception), or it is ahead of us (all civilizations eventually collapse).

Other researchers suggest that we are not communicating on the right channels. The **SETI** program listens to radio waves, but a more advanced civilization might use technologies based on neutrinos or lasers that we cannot yet detect. It is also possible that Earth is deliberately isolated, like a nature reserve, in what is called the **<zoo hypothesis>**.

Finally, the answer could be temporal: on the scale of the universe, civilizations could be like fireflies lighting up and burning out very quickly, without ever shining at the same time to see each other. Intersidereal distances, measured in light-years, impose a communication delay that makes any dialogue almost impossible.
Partie 4 Titre: The future of detection and cultural impact
Partie 4 Contenu:
The hunt for life is entering a new era thanks to instruments of unprecedented precision, such as the **James Webb** Space Telescope. It no longer just takes pictures of planets; it analyzes the interaction of light with their atmosphere through **<spectroscopy>**. This technique allows identifying the chemical composition of the air of distant worlds in search of abnormal quantities of oxygen, methane, or ozone.

The discovery of life, even purely microbial, would cause an ontological earthquake. It would prove that the appearance of life is not a unique accident, but a standard biological process of the universe. This would mean that life is written into the laws of physics and chemistry, and is not the result of a miraculous geographical chance.

In the meantime, we continue to send bottles into the cosmic sea. The **Voyager** probes, launched in 1977, carry engraved golden records containing sounds and images from Earth. Although the chances of them being intercepted are almost zero, these objects testify to our fundamental need to leave our cosmic solitude.

{If a civilization located in the Andromeda galaxy were looking at us today with an imaginary ultra-powerful telescope, it would not see humans, but the first ancestors of man 2.5 million years ago, because of the time it takes light to travel.}

|| The universe contains hundreds of billions of planets, making life statistically probable, but the absence of contact (Fermi paradox) suggests that the emergence of technological intelligence is either extremely rare or fleeting. ||

Intro: A black hole is a region of space-time where the gravitational field is so intense that the velocity required to escape it, called **escape velocity**, is greater than the speed of light. Long considered simple mathematical solutions from Albert Einstein's **General Relativity**, these fascinating objects are today an observational reality. They are not holes in the literal sense, but concentrations of matter of such density that they deform the very fabric of the universe, creating an invisible boundary beyond which no information can reach us.
Partie 1 Titre: The agony of giants and gravitational collapse
Partie 1 Contenu:
The genesis of a stellar black hole begins with the death of a massive star, possessing at least **20 to 25 times the mass of the Sun**. For millions of years, such a star survives thanks to a precarious balance between two opposing forces: **gravity**, which seeks to compress everything toward the center, and **radiation pressure** from nuclear fusion, which pushes outward.

When the star has exhausted its nuclear fuel, the radiation pressure stops abruptly. Gravity then takes over without resistance, causing the core of the star to collapse on itself in a fraction of a second. This shock releases phenomenal energy in the form of a **supernova** explosion. If the residual core is sufficiently massive (exceeding the **Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit**), no known physical force can stop the compression.

The matter is then compressed until it occupies a quasi-zero volume, reaching an infinite density: this is the **singularity**. Around this point, **<The event horizon>** forms, a spherical boundary whose radius is proportional to the object's mass. Crossing this limit means definitively leaving the accessible universe.

{If you fell into a black hole, you would undergo "spaghettification": the gravity at your feet would be so much stronger than at your head that your body would be stretched like a strand of pasta before even reaching the horizon.}
Partie 2 Titre: The mechanics of the invisible: types and operation
Partie 2 Contenu:
Contrary to a stubborn misconception, a black hole is not a vacuum cleaner of matter that travels through the universe. Its force of attraction depends solely on its mass and distance. If our Sun were suddenly replaced by a black hole of identical mass, Earth would continue its orbital trajectory without being "sucked in," although we would eventually freeze for lack of light.

Astronomers classify these objects into several categories. Besides stellar black holes, there are giants: **supermassive black holes**. Their mass varies from a few million to several billion times that of the Sun. They sit at the heart of almost all galaxies. In our own Milky Way, this role is held by **Sgr A*** (Sagittarius A-star), a monster of **4 million solar masses**.

Their presence is revealed by the influence they exert on their environment. Matter that gets too close forms an **<accretion disk>**, a ring of gas and dust swirling at speeds close to the speed of light. Friction within this disk heats the matter to millions of degrees, making it extremely bright in the X-ray and radio wave spectrum, which paradoxically allows us to "see" the shadow of the black hole against this luminous background.
Partie 3 Titre: The era of direct observation: 2019, the historical year
Partie 3 Contenu:
For decades, we only had indirect evidence of the existence of black holes. This paradigm changed in **April 2019** thanks to the **Event Horizon Telescope** (EHT) project. Using a technique called <interferometry>, researchers combined data from eight radio telescopes spread across the globe to create a virtual telescope the size of the Earth.

[black hole accretion disk galaxy]

The target was **M87***, the supermassive black hole in the Messier 87 galaxy, located **55 million light-years** away. The revealed image shows an asymmetrical ring of light surrounding a zone of total darkness: the silhouette of the event horizon. This historic shot confirmed point by point Einstein's predictions made a century earlier.

This major advance was completed in **2022** by the first image of our own neighbor, **Sgr A***. In parallel, astronomy entered a new era in **2015** with the detection, by the **LIGO** and **Virgo** observatories, of **gravitational waves**. These ripples in space-time are produced during cosmic cataclysms, such as the merger of two black holes, allowing us for the first time to "listen" to the vibrations of the universe.
Partie 4 Titre: Theoretical paradoxes and the fate of the universe
Partie 4 Contenu:
Black holes are at the heart of modern theoretical physics because they push the laws of nature to their limits. In **1974**, physicist **Stephen Hawking** revolutionized our understanding by demonstrating that black holes are not totally black. Due to quantum effects at the interface of the horizon, they would emit extremely faint radiation: **<Hawking radiation>**.

This discovery implies that a black hole very slowly loses mass over time. If it no longer absorbs anything, it eventually evaporates completely. However, for a stellar-mass black hole, this process would take billions of times the current age of the universe. This concept raises the "information paradox": if an object falls into a black hole and the latter evaporates, what happens to the information stored in the original object? Solving this enigma is one of the greatest challenges in current physics.

Whether through their role as "engines" at the heart of galaxies or their ability to warp time (which flows more slowly near an intense gravity field), black holes remain the ultimate laboratories for testing our understanding of reality. They are the missing link between the infinitely large of Relativity and the infinitely small of quantum mechanics.

|| A black hole forms by the collapse of a massive star and is delimited by the event horizon, a boundary crossed for the first time visually in 2019 with the image of M87*.||

Titre: The theory of relativity for everyone
Intro:
In 1905 and 1915, **Albert Einstein** published two theories that completely overturned our conception of space, time, and gravity. Until then, physics relied on <Newton>'s vision, where time was a river flowing in a universal and immutable way.

[Albert Einstein portrait Princeton]

By challenging these certainties, Einstein not only revolutionized our understanding of the Universe, from black holes to the Big Bang, but he also enabled the existence of everyday technologies. These theories are not just abstract physics: they have concrete applications within your smartphone.
Partie 1 Titre: Special relativity (1905): the end of absolute time
Partie 1 Contenu:
**Special relativity** (1905) proposes a radical break by basing physics on two pillars. First, the laws of nature are the same for everyone moving at a constant speed. Second, the **speed of light** in a vacuum (about 300,000 km/s) is an impassable limit and identical for everyone, whether one approaches it or moves away from it.

This constant speed of light imposes a sacrifice: that of the fixity of time. For light to maintain the same speed for two different observers, it is time itself that must adjust. This is the phenomenon of **<time dilation>**: the faster an Object moves, the slower time passes for it compared to a stationary observer. This is not an optical illusion, but a physical reality measured by atomic clocks.

The other revolution of 1905 is the equation **E=mc²**. It establishes that mass is actually "condensed" energy. Since the speed of light (c) is immense, its Square (c²) is astronomical: thus, a tiny amount of matter can release colossal energy. This discovery is the foundation of <nuclear physics>.

{Einstein published his Theory of special relativity in 1905 while working as an examiner in a patent office in Bern - without an academic post, without a laboratory, almost without a library.}
Partie 2 Titre: General relativity (1915): malleable space-time
Partie 2 Contenu:
After ten years of further reflection, Einstein extended his Theory to gravity with **general relativity**. Newton saw gravity as an invisible force acting instantly at a distance between two masses. Einstein proposed a geometric vision: space and time are not a rigid frame, but an elastic fabric called **space-time**.

Massive objects, like the Sun, deform this fabric. Imagine a bowling ball placed on a trampoline: it creates a dip. If you roll a marble next to it, it will roll toward the dip not because it is "sucked in," but because the surface is curved. For Einstein, the Earth orbits the Sun because it follows the curvature of space-time generated by the solar mass.

This Theory predicts that even light, though massless, must follow these curves. The brilliant proof was provided in **1919** by the astronomer **Arthur Eddington**. During an eclipse, he measured the position of stars located behind the Sun: their light was deflected by the solar mass, confirming that space was indeed curved. Einstein then became an instant global celebrity.

{At his death in 1955, pathologist Thomas Harvey stole Einstein's brain during the autopsy without his family's permission, keeping it in jars for decades to try to unlock the secret of his genius.}
Partie 3 Titre: From the infinitely large to the palm of your hand: GPS
Partie 3 Contenu:
The functioning of the **GPS system** is daily proof that Relativity is indispensable. Satellites orbit the Earth at 14,000 km/h and are located at an altitude of 20,000 km. To provide a position accurate to the nearest meter, the system must synchronize clocks on the ground with those on the satellites. However, two relativistic effects oppose each other here.

On one hand, the speed of the satellites causes time to pass more slowly there (effect of special relativity), leading to a delay of 7 microseconds per day. On the other hand, gravity being weaker at altitude, space-time is less curved and time passes faster there (effect of general relativity), causing an advance of 45 microseconds.

The net result is an advance of 38 microseconds per day. This seems negligible, but at the speed of light, such a shift would throw off your position by 10 to 11 kilometers after the very first day if engineers had not integrated Einstein's equations into the calculation software.

{Without relativistic corrections integrated into the calculations, your smartphone GPS would display a localization error of several kilometers after only a few hours of operation.}
Partie 4 Titre: Einstein's legacy: waves and cosmology
Partie 4 Contenu:
Beyond technical applications, Relativity opened the way to the study of the most extreme objects in the Universe. It allowed for the theorization of <black holes>, regions where the curvature of space-time is so infinite that even light cannot escape. Einstein himself doubted their actual existence, yet it is observed today by <radio astronomy>.

In 1916, he also predicted the existence of **gravitational waves**: vibrations of space-time produced by violent events, such as the collision of two black holes. These "ripples" propagate at the speed of light. It took a century for technology to be sensitive enough: in 2015, the **LIGO** interferometer detected these waves for the first time, confirming the master's final prediction.

Finally, Relativity allowed us to understand that the Universe is not static but expanding. Although Einstein initially introduced a "cosmological constant" to maintain a fixed model of the universe, he eventually recognized the expansion proven by Hubble, opening the door to the Theory of the <Big Bang>.

|| To remember: E=mc² means that energy and mass are linked; general Relativity explains that gravity curves space-time; without these calculations, your GPS would commit an error of 11 km per day. ||

Intro:
Lightning is one of the most spectacular manifestations of atmospheric energy. In a fraction of a second, a single electrical discharge releases as much energy as a car consumes in an entire week. This extreme phenomenon transforms the air, usually an insulator, into a conductive plasma heated to **30,000°C**, which is five times the temperature at the surface of the Sun.

[lightning strike storm]

Beyond its visual beauty, lightning is the result of a complex process of electrification that transforms a storm cloud into a gigantic natural battery. Whether it strikes the **Eiffel Tower**, hit an average of four times a year, or the ground in the open countryside, it follows precise physical laws that modern Science is now able to decipher, from the microscopic collision of ice crystals to the supersonic shockwave of thunder.
Partie 1 Titre: The electrical genesis within the cumulonimbus
Partie 1 Contenu:
It all starts within the **<cumulonimbus>**, the only cloud capable of generating lightning. These Giants of the atmosphere can rise up to **15 km** in altitude, passing through zones where the temperature drops well below zero. It is in this thermal forge that the **<charge separation in cumulonimbus clouds>** takes place.

Within the cloud, extremely violent updrafts bring together two types of particles: ice crystals, light and carried upward, and **<sleet>**, denser ice granules that fall due to gravity. When these particles collide, a transfer of electrons occurs via the **<triboelectric effect>**. Rising ice crystals become positively charged, while falling sleet accumulates a negative charge.

[cumulonimbus thunderstorm cloud]

This mechanism creates a dipolar structure: the top of the cloud becomes a massive positive pole and the base a negative zone. By influence, this negative base repels electrons from the ground, making the terrestrial surface positively charged just below the storm. The potential difference between the cloud and the ground then becomes colossal, often reaching **100 to 300 million volts**.

{The most struck place in the World is Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, where up to 297 storm days per year are observed, creating a near-permanent spectacle.}
Partie 2 Titre: The mechanics of discharge: from cloud to ground
Partie 2 Contenu:
Air is naturally an insulator, but when electrical voltage becomes too high, it undergoes dielectric breakdown. This is when the **<ionization of the air>** occurs: air molecules lose their electrons and become conductive. An invisible channel, called the **leader**, then shoots out from the cloud. It progresses in successive leaps of 50 meters, zigzagging to find the path of least electrical resistance.

In response to the approach of this negative leader, positive charges on the ground—particularly on pointed objects like lightning rods or trees—rise toward the sky. These are **streamers**, ascending electrical filaments. When a leader and a streamer meet, the circuit is "closed": a conductive bridge is established between sky and earth.

It is at this precise moment that the **return stroke** occurs. Contrary to popular belief, the lightning flash we see mostly travels up from the ground to the cloud. This main discharge carries a current of **30,000 amperes** at a prodigious speed, about one-third the speed of light. A complete lightning strike is often composed of several successive discharges, following one another within milliseconds in the same ionized channel, which explains the flickering effect we perceive.
Partie 3 Titre: Thunder and the physics of sound
Partie 3 Contenu:
Lightning is not only a light phenomenon; it is also a major acoustic Event. **Thunder** is the direct consequence of the extreme heat of the electric arc. Reaching **30,000°C** in record time (a few microseconds), the air within the ionized channel undergoes a sudden and violent expansion. This rapid dilation creates a supersonic shockwave that turns, as it travels away, into the sound wave we hear.

Since light travels at **300,000 km/s** and sound at only **340 m/s**, there is a time lag between visual and auditory perception. This difference allows for estimating the distance of the strike: simply count the seconds between the flash and the thunder and divide by three to get the distance in kilometers (or multiply by 340 for the exact distance in meters).

On a global scale, electrical activity is permanent. The Earth is struck by approximately **100 bolts of lightning per second**, which plays a crucial role in maintaining the electrical balance of the atmosphere. Without these discharges, the Earth's electric field would quickly vanish. In France, there are about **one million** ground strikes every year, mainly during the summer Period.
Partie 4 Titre: Risks, extremes, and statistics
Partie 4 Contenu:
Lightning remains a real danger, although statistically Rare for an individual. It is estimated that the probability of being struck by lightning over an 80-year lifetime is **1 in 15,000**. Every year, about **2,000 people** lose their lives to this phenomenon in the World. Most accidents occur during plein air activities, when victims become, due to their height or isolation, the starting point for a positive streamer.

In addition to human damage, lightning has a significant ecological impact, being the cause of many natural forest fires. However, it plays a little-known beneficial role: the energy of the lightning bolt breaks down nitrogen molecules in the air, allowing the formation of nitrogen compounds that fall with the rain and naturally fertilize the soil.

STudy of lightning continues to reveal strange phenomena, such as **upper-atmospheric lightning** ( <Sprites> or <Elves>) which occur above clouds and are only visible from space or through ultra-fast cameras. These discoveries remind us that we only perceive a tiny fraction of our planet's electrical activity.

{Roy Sullivan, an American park ranger, holds the World record after being struck by lightning seven times between 1942 and 1977. He survived each of these electrical encounters.}

|| To remember: Lightning comes from a separation of charges (ice (+) / sleet (-)) in a cumulonimbus, creating an ionized channel at 30,000°C whose sudden expansion generates the thunder shockwave. ||

Intro: The <greenhouse effect> is often presented in public debate as a recent environmental threat or pollution generated by humans. \n\nHowever, the scientific reality is more nuanced: the greenhouse effect is above all a **natural phenomenon essential** to the emergence and maintenance of life on Earth. Without it, our planet would be nothing but an icy desert. The real contemporary issue does not lie in the existence of this mechanism, but in its brutal **amplification** by human activities, which breaks a climatic balance of several millennia.
Partie 1 Titre: The natural greenhouse effect: a vital thermal shield
Partie 1 Contenu:
To understand the importance of this phenomenon, one must imagine the Earth without an atmosphere. Without the greenhouse effect, the average temperature at the globe's surface would drop to approximately **-18°C**, making liquid water impossible and life as we know it non-existent. Thanks to this process, the current average stands at **+15°C**.

The mechanism relies on the planet's **radiative balance**. The Sun bombards the Earth with high-energy radiation (mostly visible light). The atmosphere is largely transparent to these short waves, which reach the ground and warm it. In return, to evacuate this energy, the Earth emits infrared radiation (heat) towards space.

This is where **<greenhouse gases>** come into play. Unlike the majority gases in the air (nitrogen and oxygen), these molecules have the physical property of absorbing long-wavelength infrared radiation. They trap this heat and re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the Earth's surface. This "recycling" of thermal energy maintains the lower atmosphere at a mild temperature.

 The term "greenhouse effect" is physically inaccurate: a real garden greenhouse heats up primarily by physically preventing warm air from escaping through convection, whereas the atmosphere heats up through radiative interaction.
Partie 2 Titre: The anthropogenic greenhouse effect: the breaking of the balance
Partie 2 Contenu:
Since the industrial revolution, the natural balance has been disturbed by the massive addition of gases of human origin, known as **anthropogenic**. The primary source is the combustion of **fossil fuels** (coal, oil, natural gas). This process releases carbon into the atmosphere that had been sequestered underground for hundreds of millions of years, thus injecting a massive surplus into the short carbon cycle.

[factory chimneys greenhouse gas emissions]

Human activities act on several levers. Massive **deforestation** reduces natural "carbon sinks" capable of absorbing CO₂ through photosynthesis. Simultaneously, **industrial livestock farming** and rice cultivation emit methane (CH₄). Although less abundant than CO₂, methane is a much more efficient gas at trapping heat, with a global warming potential approximately **80 times more powerful** over a 20-year period.

The figures are undeniable: the atmospheric concentration of CO₂ has risen from **280 ppm** (parts per million) in the 18th century to over **420 ppm** in the 21st century. Such a concentration level has not been observed on Earth since the **Pliocene**, about 3 million years ago, a time when temperatures and sea levels were much higher than today.
Partie 3 Titre: Systemic consequences and scientific consensus
Partie 3 Contenu:
The study of this phenomenon is coordinated at the global level by the **<IPCC>**. This body does not produce its own research but synthesizes the work of thousands of climatologists. Its conclusions are formal: the warming observed since 1950 is unprecedented over millennia and its human origin is established with almost absolute certainty.

The increase in energy stored in the atmosphere modifies the global dynamics of the climate. We observe an intensification of the water cycle, leading to more marked contrasts: dry areas become more arid, while humid areas experience more violent precipitation. The melting of ice caps and mountain glaciers, coupled with the thermal expansion of heated water, leads to an inexorable rise in ocean levels.

Another aggravating factor is the modification of the **<terrestrial albedo>**. As they melt, white surfaces (snow, ice) that reflected sunlight give way to dark surfaces (earth, ocean) that absorb heat. This mechanism creates a positive feedback loop: the warmer it gets, the more ice melts, and the more energy the Earth absorbs, accelerating the initial warming even further.

 The planet Venus is the extreme example of a "runaway" greenhouse effect: its atmosphere, composed of 96% CO₂, traps so much heat that the ground temperature reaches 460°C, enough to melt lead.
Partie 4 Titre: Perspectives and transition levers
Partie 4 Contenu:
Faced with this observation, the international community is trying to organize to limit warming to **+1.5°C** or **+2°C** compared to the pre-industrial era. These thresholds are not arbitrary: they aim to avoid irreversible tipping points, such as the thawing of the **<permafrost>**, which could release colossal amounts of methane trapped in the frozen soils of Siberia and Alaska.

The fight against the amplification of the greenhouse effect relies on two pillars: **mitigation** and **adaptation**. Mitigation consists of reducing emissions at the source through the decarbonization of energy, energy efficiency, and sobriety. Adaptation aims to prepare societies for changes that are already inevitable (flood-resistant infrastructure, selection of heat-resilient crops).

The challenge is immense because greenhouse gases have a long lifespan in the atmosphere. The CO₂ emitted today will continue to influence the climate for centuries. This requires immediate and structural action on our production and consumption models to stabilize the chemical composition of our atmosphere and preserve the conditions for the habitability of the biosphere.

|| Without the natural greenhouse effect, the Earth would be an icy desert at -18°C. Its current amplification by fossil fuels is propelling CO₂ concentrations to levels unseen for 3 million years, threatening the global climatic balance. ||

Intro:
We spend about **one-third of our existence** in a state of apparent unconsciousness: sleep. For a 75-year life, this represents nearly **25 years** of rest. Long perceived as a simple phase of inactivity or a waste of time, sleep proves to be a biological process of fascinating complexity.

[sleeping person bedroom night]

Although every animal species devotes a significant portion of its energy to it, sciences are still seeking to unlock the mystery of its ultimate functions. Yet, one certainty remains: sleep is an absolute vital necessity, just like water or food. This course explores the mechanisms that make our nights the essential engine of our daytime performance and health.
Partie 1 Titre: Proof by absence: the risks of deprivation
Partie 1 Contenu:
The most radical method for understanding the utility of a biological function is to observe the consequences of its disappearance. The historical experiment of **Randy Gardner** in 1964 remains a reference: after **11 days** without sleeping, this student exhibited major cognitive disorders, visual hallucinations, and severe paranoia, illustrating the rapid collapse of the mental architecture.

Beyond the psychological sphere, sleep deprivation attacks the organism as a whole. Studies conducted on rats have shown that a total lack of rest leads to death in just **2 to 3 weeks**, a timeframe identical to that of strict food deprivation. In humans, this fatality is observed in an extremely Rare genetic pathology: **fatal familial insomnia**, where the impossibility of falling into sleep inevitably leads to death within a few months due to multi-organ failure.

In daily life, lack of sleep alters our abilities in an insidious way. It is estimated that driving after 17 hours of active wakefulness is equivalent to a blood alcohol level of 0.5 g/l, which is the **legal intoxication** threshold in many countries. Vigilance drops, reaction times lengthen, and the brain undergoes uncontrollable <microsleeps>, proving that the need to sleep always ends up imposing itself over will.

{In 1964, after his record of 264 hours without sleep, Randy Gardner slept for 14 hours straight and woke up perfectly functional, although his rapid eye movement sleep cycle took several weeks to fully stabilize.}
Partie 2 Titre: Maintenance and cleaning: the brain's nightly workshop
Partie 2 Contenu:
While we sleep, the brain does not turn off; it changes its operating mode to prioritize maintenance. One of the best-documented functions is **memory consolidation**. It is during the night that the hippocampus transfers volatile information from the day to the <Neocortex> for long-term storage. This reorganization allows for an increase in learning performance by 20 to 40% compared to an equivalent period of wakefulness.

On a physical level, deep sleep acts as a true repairer. It is during this phase that **growth hormone** is secreted massively. Contrary to its name, it is not just for children: in adults, it is responsible for protein synthesis, the repair of muscle micro-lesions, and the strengthening of the immune system via the production of <cytokines>.

Finally, a major discovery of the last decade concerns the <Glymphatic system>. This drainage network, ten times more active during sleep, uses cerebrospinal fluid to flush out toxins accumulated by neuronal activity.

[brain glymphatic sleep cerebrospinal fluid]

Among these waste products are **beta-amyloid proteins**. In cases of chronic deprivation, these proteins clump together and form plaques, which considerably increases the risks of developing **Alzheimer's** disease in the long term.

{While you sleep, your brain cells contract by about 60% to facilitate the circulation of cerebrospinal fluid and allow for more efficient cleaning of toxins by the glymphatic system.}
Partie 3 Titre: Evolutionary diversity: strategies of the living
Partie 3 Contenu:
Sleep is a universal trait that transcends species, but its form adapts to environmental constraints. In the animal kingdom, the duration of rest is often correlated with the position in the food chain. Predators, like **cats**, can afford to sleep between **12 to 16 hours** per day without immediate fear. Conversely, vulnerable herbivores like **giraffes** settle for **30 minutes to 2 hours** daily, divided into standing micro-naps to be able to flee instantly.

Some species have developed spectacular mechanisms to reconcile survival and rest. **Dolphins** and certain birds practice **uni-hemispheric sleep**: only one cerebral hemisphere sleeps while the Other remains vigilant. This allows cetaceans to rise to the surface to breathe and migratory birds to maintain their trajectory during transatlantic flights of several days.

Humans, for their part, show a notable evolution according to age. **Babies** sleep up to 18 hours a day, with a predominance of <rapid eye movement sleep>. This phase, where brain activity is intense and dreams are frequent, is crucial for <synaptogenesis>, meaning the creation of connections between neurons that structure future intelligence.
Partie 4 Titre: {Sea otters sometimes sleep while holding hands (paws) to keep from drifting away and losing each other while they sleep in ocean currents.}
Partie 4 Contenu: Regulation and lifestyle hygiene: the internal clock

Titre: How does the brain store memories?
Intro: Human memory is nothing like a static hard drive or a library of filed records. It is a dynamic process, a living and plastic network composed of billions of nerve cells that reconnect, strengthen, or wither according to our experiences. Far from being localized in a single point, it mobilizes several brain structures working in concert to transform a fleeting perception into lasting knowledge. Understanding the biological mechanisms of memory, from the microscopic scale of the synapse to the complex coordination of the hippocampus, allows us not only to optimize our learning but also to take a more accurate look at the fragility of our identity and the pathologies that alter it.
Partie 1 Titre: The microscopic scale: synaptic plasticity
Partie 1 Contenu:
At the base of every memory are **synapses**, those chemical communication zones located between neurons. The human brain houses about **86 billion neurons**, and each of them can establish thousands of contacts with its neighbors, creating a staggering network of more than **100 trillion synapses**.

[neuron synapse microscopy fluorescence]

When information circulates through this network for the first time, it follows a specific electrical path. If this information is repeated or associated with a strong emotion, the neurons involved fire together repeatedly. This is where **<long-term potentiation>** (LTP) comes in. This mechanism, postulated by neurophysiologist **Donald Hebb**, relies on a simple principle: the simultaneous stimulation of two neurons strengthens the efficiency of their synaptic transmission. In other words, the more a circuit is used, the "easier" the connection becomes to activate.

This plasticity allows the brain to physically modify its structure to store information. A memory is therefore not a stored object, but a biological trace left by the synchronized activation of a group of cells. It is the strength of these links that determines whether information will be forgotten in seconds or kept for a lifetime.

{The human brain has an estimated storage capacity of 2.5 petabytes, which is equivalent to about three million hours of television shows, or more than 300 years of non-stop viewing.}
Partie 2 Titre: The hippocampus, architect of consolidation
Partie 2 Contenu:
If synapses are the tools of memory, **the hippocampus** is its main architect. This small structure nestled at the heart of the <temporal lobe> plays a "stationmaster" role for conscious memories, whether they are life stories or general knowledge.

[hippocampus memory brain]

The hippocampus does not store memories permanently. Its role is to receive them, encode them, and redistribute them to the **cerebral cortex**. This transfer is called the **consolidation** process. During this phase, the hippocampus literally "replays" the neural sequences experienced during the day to carve them lastingly into the upper layers of the brain.

Scientific research has shown that consolidation occurs mainly during **sleep**, and particularly during the REM sleep phase. It is at this moment that information passes from a fragile and unstable state to a permanent and robust state. Without a functional hippocampus, an individual can experience things, but is unable to fix them. They remain a prisoner of a perpetual present, unable to project themselves into the future because they lack a recent past.

{Henry Molaison, known as patient H.M., lost the ability to form new memories in 1953, but he could learn to draw in a mirror better and better each day, even though he claimed each time that he had never practiced this exercise.}
Partie 3 Titre: Malleability: when the brain performs a Reconstruction of the past
Partie 3 Contenu:
A common error is to believe that remembering is like consulting a video recording. In reality, the recall of a memory is an **active Reconstruction**. Each time we access a piece of information, it becomes unstable and can be modified by our current emotions, our new knowledge, or the suggestions of our environment before being "recorded" again in the brain.

Psychologist **Elizabeth Loftus** revolutionized this field by demonstrating the ease with which **false memories** can be implanted. Through simple suggestive questions, she managed to persuade subjects that they had experienced totally imaginary childhood events, such as being lost in a shopping mall or witnessing an accident.

This malleability has profound consequences, particularly in the field of Law. Eyewitness testimonies, once considered irrefutable evidence, are now approached with caution. We now know that the human mind can, in good faith, invent details or modify faces to fill gaps in memory or respond to social or judicial pressure.

{The Mandela effect is a phenomenon of collective false memories where thousands of people share an identical erroneous memory, such as the Monopoly Figure wearing a monocle, when he never had one.}
Partie 4 Titre: The diversity of memory systems
Partie 4 Contenu:
The brain does not handle all memories in the same way. We generally distinguish two major systems: explicit (or declarative) memory and implicit (non-declarative) memory. The first concerns facts and events that can be named. It is divided into **episodic memory** (our personal memories) and **semantic memory** (our internal dictionary of concepts).

In contrast, **<procedural memory>** manages motor automatisms and skills. Unlike memories managed by the hippocampus, this memory of gestures depends on more primitive structures like the **cerebellum** and the **basal ganglia**. It is thanks to it that we never forget how to ride a bike or swim, even after years without practice.

This separation explains why some patients with profound amnesia can forget their own name but keep intact their ability to play a complex musical instrument. Memory is therefore not a monolithic entity, but a mosaic of specialized functions, each anchored in a specific region of our neural architecture.

|| The memory is not a static file but a dynamic biological trace resulting from the reinforcement of synaptic connections and their nocturnal consolidation. ||

Intro: Certain organisms defy our fundamental Concept of biology by challenging the inevitability of death. While humans seem programmed to decline, the jellyfish <Turritopsis dohrnii> possesses the astounding ability to reset its biological clock to rejuvenate indefinitely. Longevity records, such as that of the quahog clam **Ming** which lived for **507 years**, suggest that senescence is not a universal Law of the living but a plastic process. By studying these exceptions, sciences seek to understand if aging is a biological fatality or a simple molecular engineering problem that could be solved.
Partie 1 Titre: The erosion of the living: the mechanisms of senescence
Partie 1 Contenu:
**Aging**, or senescence, is not a passive process of wear and tear similar to a machine rusting. It is the result of an imbalance between the accumulation of cellular damage and the capacity of the organism to repair it.

At the heart of this process are <telomeres>. At each cell division, the replication machinery fails to copy the ultimate end of the DNA. To protect vital genetic information, chromosomes are equipped with these protective "caps" composed of repetitive sequences. However, these structures shorten at each cycle. When they reach a critical size, the cell enters **senescence**: it stops dividing to avoid corrupting its genetic code.

[chromosome DNA telomere aging cell]

{The tardigrade, or 'water bear', can enter a state of cryptobiosis by drying out almost completely. In this state, its metabolism stops by 99.99%, allowing it to survive the vacuum of space, extreme temperatures, or lethal radiation for decades without aging.}

At the same time, the organism undergoes the constant assault of **free radicals**, unstable molecules produced by metabolism that damage proteins and lipids. If DNA replication errors accumulate, they can lead to apoptosis (programmed cell death) or, worse, cancerous mutations. **Senescent cells**, although unable to divide, do not necessarily die; they accumulate and secrete inflammatory factors that poison the tissue environment, accelerating the decline of nearby healthy cells.
Partie 2 Titre: The champions of biological resilience
Partie 2 Contenu:
Some species have developed strategies to bypass these limits. The most famous example is that of the jellyfish <Turritopsis dohrnii>. Unlike other jellyfish that die after reproduction, it is capable of **transdifferentiation**. When faced with injury or starvation, it transforms its specialized adult cells into pluripotent stem cells. It thus returns to the polyp state, starting its development from scratch. This inverted life cycle allows for a form of **biological immortality**.

In a different register, the **Hydra**, a small freshwater polyp, shows no measurable signs of aging. Its secret lies in a quasi-unlimited stock of <stem cells> that renew its entire body every twenty days. As long as the environment remains stable, the Hydra does not die of old age.

{Lobsters possess an enzyme called telomerase in all their tissues, which prevents their telomeres from ever shortening. They thus grow throughout their lives and become more fertile with age; they only die because their growth eventually makes molting too exhausting or impossible.}

Finally, the **bowhead whale** illustrates another strategy: cancer resistance. Although it has billions more cells than humans, it lives over 200 years thanks to a duplication of specific genes dedicated to ultra-efficient DNA repair and cell cycle regulation.
Partie 3 Titre: Towards a medicine of causes rather than symptoms
Partie 3 Contenu:
The study of these species inspires new approaches for human anti-aging medicine. The objective is no longer just to treat age-related diseases (Alzheimer's, cancers, osteoarthritis), but to tackle the process of aging itself as a root pathology.

The path of **senolytics** is one of the most promising. These molecules are designed to force senescent cells, those "zombie cells" that refuse to die, to self-destruct. By purging tissues of these inflammatory focuses, researchers have succeeded, in animal models, in restoring youthful functions and extending healthy life expectancy.

Another path concerns **caloric restriction**. It has been observed that limiting energy intake without malnutrition activates **sirtuins**, proteins that supervise cellular health. This mechanism puts the organism in "survival and repair" mode rather than "growth and reproduction" mode, inhibiting the <mTOR> pathway which, when overactive, accelerates cellular decline.

Finally, in vivo **cellular reprogramming** attempts to mimic the process of the immortal jellyfish. By temporarily activating specific transcription factors (Yamanaka factors), scientists hope to reset the epigenetic age of our cells without turning them into tumors, opening the way to the regeneration of entire organs.
Partie 4 Titre: The limits of immortality: ethics and environment
Partie 4 Contenu:
Biological immortality does not mean invulnerability. In nature, even a biologically immortal species eventually dies from predation, disease, or climate change. Death remains an essential engine of **evolution**: it allows for the renewal of generations and genetic adaptation to environmental changes. Without death, natural selection would stop, freezing species in a state unsuited to future challenges.

For humanity, the perspective of radically slowing down aging raises dizzying ethical questions. If longevity becomes a technology, it risks accentuating **social inequalities**, creating a caste of wealthy individuals capable of living for centuries. Furthermore, a massive extension of lifespan would pose problems of overpopulation and resource management on a planet with limited capacities.

Nevertheless, the primary ambition of current research remains "healthspan" (healthy life expectancy) rather than "lifespan" (total life expectancy). The challenge is to reduce the time spent in dependency and illness at the end of life. The dream of eternal youth, inspired by the marine abysses, pushes us to redefine what it means to be human in a World where finitude would no longer be an absolute rule.

|| Biological immortality rests on the ability of certain cells to repair DNA or to reset themselves, like the jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii which practices transdifferentiation to rejuvenate. ||

Intro:
Photosynthesis is the fundamental biochemical process by which autotrophic organisms, such as green plants, algae, and certain bacteria, **convert sunlight into chemical energy** stored as carbohydrates.

[leaf photosynthesis sunlight chloroplasts]

This mechanism constitutes the cornerstone of almost all life on Earth, as it is the source of biomass and atmospheric oxygen. Without this reaction, initiated billions of years ago by primitive micro-organisms, the energy dynamics of our planet would be non-existent and complex life, as we know it, could never have emerged.
Partie 1 Titre: The site of the reaction: chloroplasts
Partie 1 Contenu:
To understand photosynthesis, one must dive into the heart of the plant cell, into specialized organelles called **chloroplasts**. These structures contain stacks of membranes named thylakoids, which house **<chlorophyll>**, the pigment responsible for capturing solar photons.

[chloroplast plant cell green]

The chemical functioning can be summarized by a precise equation: **6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + 6O₂**. Plants draw Carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the air via the <stomata>, tiny pores located on the surface of leaves, while water (H₂O) is transported from the roots.

The glucose produced serves as a building block for the plant (growth, fruits, roots), while oxygen is released.

{If plants appear green to us, it is because chlorophyll reflects the green wavelengths of the light spectrum; it prefers to absorb the energy of blue and red lights, which are more efficient at exciting its electrons.}
Partie 2 Titre: The mechanics of the two phases: light and synthesis
Partie 2 Contenu:
Photosynthesis is not a single instantaneous reaction, but a series of transformations divided into two distinct stages. The first, the **photochemical phase** (or light-dependent phase), takes place in the thylakoid membranes. Here, solar energy is used to break water molecules, a process called photolysis. This stage releases oxygen and produces two essential energy-carrying molecules: **ATP** and **NADPH**.

The second stage, the **chemical phase** (or dark phase), occurs in the stroma of the chloroplast and uses the products of the first phase. This stage centers on the **<Calvin cycle>**, named after the chemist **Melvin Calvin**.

During this cycle, the carbon from CO₂ is "fixed" to form glucose through a complex series of enzymatic reactions. Although this phase does not require direct light to function, it depends entirely on the energy accumulated during the day. It is here that the plant truly transforms carbon dioxide into solid organic matter.

{Melvin Calvin had to use radioactive carbon isotopes, a technology derived from research on the atomic bomb, to map the path of carbon in the plant, which earned him the Nobel Prize in 1961.}
Partie 3 Titre: The Great Oxidation: a planetary shift
Partie 3 Contenu:
About 2.4 billion years ago, the Earth experienced a major geochemical rupture. The first photosynthetic bacteria, **cyanobacteria**, began to release oxygen massively into an environment that was then devoid of it.

This Event, known as the **"Great Oxidation"**, radically changed the composition of the atmosphere. Initially, oxygen was a poison for the anaerobic organisms of the time. But its accumulation allowed for the creation of the ozone layer and favored the emergence of cellular respiration, a much more efficient mode of energy production for living beings.

Today, the oxygen we breathe is nothing more than the accumulated "waste" of billions of years of planetary photosynthetic activity.

{About 50% of the Earth's oxygen is produced not by terrestrial forests, but by oceanic phytoplankton, making the oceans the primary lung of the World.}
Partie 4 Titre: Optimized yield and climate stakes
Partie 4 Contenu:
Although vital, natural photosynthesis is a process with modest energy yields from a thermodynamic point of view: only **1 to 3%** of the solar energy received by a leaf is actually converted into biomass. Yet, on a global scale, this yield is enough to maintain the gas balance of the Earth.

In the current context of global warming, photosynthesis plays a crucial regulatory role by acting as a **carbon sink**. Plants absorb billions of tons of anthropogenic CO₂ every year. Understanding this mechanism now allows us to imagine solutions like "artificial photosynthesis" or massive reforestation to limit the greenhouse effect.

{There is a sea slug, Elysia chlorotica, capable of "stealing" chloroplasts from the algae it eats to photosynthesize its own energy, thus becoming an animal functioning partially on solar energy.}

|| Photosynthesis is the only biological process capable of recycling mineral carbon into organic matter while regenerating the atmospheric oxygen necessary for aerobic life. ||

Intro: Why do leaves change color?
Partie 1 Titre:
Every autumn, forest landscapes transform into a mosaic of blazing colors, turning from emerald green to shades of gold, copper, and purple. This natural spectacle, far from being a simple aesthetic accident, results from a complex survival strategy and a cascade of biochemical reactions programmed by trees.

[autumn forest foliage colors red yellow]

This phenomenon is not a spontaneous creation of new colors, but rather a process of revelation and dismantling. By understanding plant physiology, we discover that autumn colors testify to the ability of trees to recycle their resources to face winter, a Period of dormancy when water freezes and solar energy becomes scarce.
Partie 1 Contenu: The dominance and decline of chlorophyll
Partie 2 Titre:
During the growth Period, from spring to late summer, leaves are saturated with **chlorophyll**. This indispensable pigment ensures **photosynthesis**, a chemical process used to convert sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into carbohydrates (energy). It is the high concentration of chlorophyll that gives leaves their characteristic green hue.

However, chlorophyll is a fragile molecule that constantly breaks down under the effect of intense light. In summer, the tree synthesizes it continuously to compensate for this loss. But leaves do not just contain green: they also house **carotenoids** (responsible for yellow and orange hues) and **xanthophylls**. These auxiliary pigments help capture other light wavelengths and protect the chlorophyll against excessive oxidation.

Throughout the summer, these warm colors are present but totally masked by the abundance of the green pigment. When autumn comes, the biochemical balance shifts: the plant stops producing chlorophyll. As existing chlorophyll molecules break down without being replaced, the green fades, finally revealing the carotenoids that had been waiting in the shadows since the start of the season.

{The word chlorophyll comes from the Greek 'chloros' (green) and 'phyllon' (leaf), while carotenoid shares the same etymology as the carrot, where this pigment was first identified.}
Partie 2 Contenu: The signal of winter: photoreceptors and abscission
Partie 3 Titre:
The trigger for this metamorphosis is not solely the cold, contrary to popular belief, but mainly **photoperiodism**. Trees measure the length of the nights thanks to light-sensitive molecules called **phytochromes**. When the nights lengthen significantly, a hormonal signal is sent to the base of each leaf.

This signal triggers the development of a <separation zone>, also called the **abscission zone**. A barrier of specialized cells, similar to a cork plug, begins to form at the junction point between the petiole and the branch. This layer progressively interrupts the flow of sap: water no longer rises to the leaf, and the sugars produced can no longer descend to the roots.

[leaf color change autumn chlorophyll]

Isolated from the rest of the tree, the leaf's metabolism stops. The breakdown of chlorophyll then accelerates because it is no longer supplied with essential minerals, notably magnesium. The yellow and orange pigments, which are more chemically stable, persist for a few weeks longer, creating the famous golden foliage before the leaf totally dries out and falls under the effect of wind or gravity.
Partie 3 Contenu: The enigma of red pigments: anthocyanins
Partie 4 Titre:
While yellows and oranges are revealed pigments, the shades of scarlet red and purple, characteristic of maples for example, are the result of active synthesis. They come from <anthocyanins>, pigments that are only produced at the end of the season, often when sugars remain trapped in the leaf because of the blocking of this <separation zone>.

Why would a plant invest energy to manufacture new pigments just before getting rid of its leaves? The answer lies in **photoprotection**. During autumn, the tree proceeds with an orderly dismantling of the leaf's cellular structures to recover vital nutrients, such as **nitrogen**, and store them in its roots.

In the absence of chlorophyll, sunlight can damage the tissues of the still-active leaf, which would disrupt this recycling. By producing anthocyanins, the tree installs a sort of "sun filter" or thermal shield. This pigment protects cells from oxidative stress, allowing the leaf to function just long enough for the tree to build up its reserves before the final fall. This is one of the most fascinating examples of resource-efficient management in the plant World.
Partie 4 Contenu: The influence of climate on the intensity of the spectacle

Intro: **Dark matter** represents one of the most dizzying challenges in contemporary astrophysics. While we thought we understood the universe through the light of stars and galaxies, 20th-century observations revealed that the vast majority of the cosmos's mass is totally invisible. Accounting for approximately **27% of the universe**, this mysterious substance does not shine, reflects no light, and blocks no radiation. It is detectable only through its gravitational influence on visible matter, acting like an invisible glue without which galaxies would fly apart. To dive into the study of dark matter is to accept that everything we see - from planets to galaxy superclusters - represents only a tiny fraction of physical reality.
Partie 1 Titre: The Rubin anomaly: galaxies following a too-fast pace
Partie 1 Contenu:
The modern History of dark matter took root in the 1970s with the work of American astronomer **Vera Rubin**. By observing the **<Galaxy rotation curve>** of spirals, she expected to find behavior similar to that of our solar system: the further an object is from the center of mass, the slower its orbital speed. However, her measurements revealed a total paradox.

[Vera Rubin astronomer telescope]

Stars located at the periphery of galaxies rotate **at the same speed**, or even faster, than those located near the galactic center. According to the laws of **universal gravitation**, these peripheral stars should be ejected into the intergalactic void because the visible mass (stars and gas) does not generate enough gravity to hold them at such speeds.

For the galactic structure to remain stable, there must exist a massive invisible component, surrounding the galaxy in the form of a **Halo**, exerting the missing gravitational force. This finding transformed a theoretical curiosity from the 1930s into an observational certainty: the universe is filled with an unknown matter.

{In the 1940s, Vera Rubin was the only female graduate in astronomy from Vassar College, but she was denied admission to Princeton for her doctorate because the university did not accept women into that program until 1975.}
Partie 2 Titre: The hunt for particles: from WIMPs to axions
Partie 2 Contenu:
Once the existence of dark matter was accepted through its effects, the question of its nature became central. We know today that it is not composed of ordinary (**Baryonic**) matter, as it does not react to electromagnetic forces. It literally passes through the Earth and our bodies without leaving a trace.

The most serious candidate for a long time was the **WIMP** (Weakly Interacting Massive Particle). It would be a heavy particle, originating from physics beyond the **<Standard Model of physics>**, interacting only through gravity and the weak nuclear force. To detect them, scientists have built giant tanks filled with liquid xenon, buried deep underground to isolate them from cosmic radiation, hoping that a WIMP will eventually collide with an atomic nucleus.

[dark matter galaxy cluster]

Failing detection after decades of hunting, Other paths are emerging. The **axion**, an extremely light particle, has become a leading candidate. Other researchers are exploring the path of **modified gravity**, suggesting that our current equations of physics are incomplete on a galactic scale. In any case, dark matter leaves an undeniable signature: it curves space-time, creating **<gravitational lenses>** that distort the image of distant galaxies located behind it.
Partie 3 Titre: Dark energy: the repulsive force
Partie 3 Contenu:
If dark matter attracts matter through gravity, **<Dark energy>** produces the opposite effect. Discovered in 1998 during the study of distant supernovae, this mysterious force is responsible for the **acceleration of the expansion** of the universe. While gravity should normally slow down this expansion, cosmologists have observed that galaxies are moving away from each other faster and faster.

This phenomenon earned the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for **Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt, and Adam Riess**. Dark energy is not just present; it dominates the cosmos. It would represent **68% of the universe**, acting as a negative pressure inherent in the space vacuum itself.

The balance is fascinating: dark matter tries to bring structures together, while Dark energy tends to disperse them. Together, these two unknowns represent **95% of the universe**. The World as we see it, made of atoms, light, and life, is but a foam of **5%** floating on an ocean of invisible darkness.

{Dark energy is so powerful that, in a very distant future, it could stretch the universe to the point that all other galaxies would become invisible from the Milky Way, leaving our descendants in a totally empty sky.}
Partie 4 Titre: Assessment: towards a new physics
Partie 4 Contenu:
The understanding of the cosmos currently faces a wall.
